summary: Overview On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497 , an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x , 24.x , and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), gives it a critical CVSSv4 score of 9.2 . An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory. According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder. As of October 26, 2026, Rapid7 is not aware of exploitation in the wild, and CVE-2026-111497 is not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog . However, given the vulnerability's potential to disclose memory or enable remote code execution (RCE), Rapid7 recommends that organizations prioritize remediation. Technical overview CVE-2026-111497 is classified as an out-of-bounds write ( CWE-787 ) and an unchecked return value ( CWE-252 ). Per the vendor advisory, the decoder handled an invalid Brotli block switch as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error. The streaming decoder then continued appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, allowing malformed input to write beyond the buffer and corrupt process memory. The vulnerability originates in Google Brotli, which the affected Node.js release lines bundle as a dependency. The CVE record identifies affected upstream Brotli ranges on all platforms as versions 1.0.3 before 1.0.10 , 1.1.0 before 1.1.1 , and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1 . The Node.js Project remediated its bundled decoder in the fixed Node.js releases listed below. Because CVE-2026-111497 affects the upstream Google Brotli decoder, its reach is not limited to Node.js. Vendor and project advisories have also identified affected implementations in Bun , Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, .NET , Envoy and Istio , brotli4j , and operating-system packages . Affected versions, default exposure, and remediation vary by product; the presence of an affected decoder does not by itself establish exposure unless an application processes attacker-controlled Brotli data. Organizations should consult the relevant downstream vendor or distribution advisories to identify affected versions, assess exposure, and determine appropriate remediation. Mitigation guidance Vendor-supplied security updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-111497. Organizations running an affected Node.js release should upgrade on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles: Node.js 22.x releases before 22.23.4 are affected; upgrade to 22.23.4 or later. Node.js 24.x releases before 24.22.1 are affected; upgrade to 24.22.1 or later. Node.js 26.x releases before 26.12.1 are affected; upgrade to 26.12.1 or later. The vendor states that end-of-life Node.js release lines should also be treated as affected when a security release occurs. Organizations using an end-of-life release should migrate to a supported, fixed release line. Node.js has not published a vendor-supported workaround; if an immediate upgrade is not possible, Rapid7 recommends restricting or disabling application paths that decompress untrusted Brotli data as a temporary exposure-reduction measure. For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the Node.js security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497 with an authenticated vulnerability check for Linux, macOS, and Windows, available in the October 26 content release. Updates October 26, 2026 : Initial publication. October 26, 2026 : Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to reflect coverage availability.

summary: CVEs: CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 Severity: Critical Executive Summary Two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable web servers, including systems hosting WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla applications. Security researchers have reported exploitation attempts surrounding the October 21 emergency security release, including activity observed before public disclosure, while VulnCheck documented automated scanning and an unsuccessful attempt to deploy a web shell through PHP session-handling functionality. With millions of internet-facing PHP deployments potentially exposed and a substantial proportion running unsupported versions, organizations face an urgent need to remediate vulnerable systems and investigate suspicious activity preceding the security release.

summary: Advisory at a Glance Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware Original Publication October 20, 2026 Executive Summary This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Next, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks. Affected Products CVE-2020-3259 [ Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor ] CVE-2023-20269 [ CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel ] CVE-2023-27532 [ CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function ] CVE-2024-40711 [ CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data ] CVE-2024-40766 [ CWE-284: Improper Access Control ] Key Actions Regularly patch and update systems, especially firewalls, and other edge devices. Implement Zero Trust Principle. Restrict administrative tools and privileges to necessary users only. Strengthen account security by implementing identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies and multifactor authentication (MFA). Indicators of Compromise For a downloadable copy of indicators of compromise, see: AA26-293A STIX XML (40 KB) AA26-293A STIX JSON (38 KB) Intended Audience Organizations: Government; Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB); State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT); Critical Infrastructure Roles: Defensive cybersecurity analysts , vulnerability analysts , security systems managers , and operational technology (OT) owners and operators Introduction Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), United States Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency, and the United Kingdom’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit—hereafter referred to as the authoring agencies—are releasing this joint advisory to disseminate known SafePay ransomware TTPs and IOCs identified through FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations as recently as August 2026. Since August 2024, SafePay ransomware group’s operations have affected a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay ransomware was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026. The SafePay threat actors have impacted at least 600 separate victims from multiple critical infrastructure sectors. The authoring agencies encourage organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this advisory to reduce the likelihood and impact of SafePay ransomware incidents. Download the PDF version of this report: #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware (PDF, 1.06 MB ) For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see: AA26-293A-STIX XML (XML, 40.23 KB ) AA26-293A-STIX JSON (JSON, 37.49 KB ) Technical Details Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK ® Matrix for Enterprise framework, version 20. See MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section of this advisory for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques. Initial Access The FBI, USSS, and cybersecurity researchers observed SafePay threat actors obtaining initial access [ TA0001 ] to organizations through various means, including credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks [ T1110 ], and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access. SafePay threat actors use the IP addresses of the VPN provider “Mullvad” to attain initial access—specifically, SafePay threat actors use phished account profiles to access victim networks to exploit the following known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) for edge device products: CVE-2020-3259 [ Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor ] CVE-2023-20269 [ CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel ] Additionally, the authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors exploiting the following vulnerabilities across internet-exposed systems [ T1190 ] for initial access through automated scripts: CVE-2023-27532 [ CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function ] CVE-2024-40711 [ CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data ] CVE-2024-40766 [ CWE-284: Improper Access Control ] Execution, Persistence, Stealth, and Defense Impairment After SafePay threat actors gain access to a victim network, they establish persistence by gaining administrative privileges on existing accounts [ T1098 ], or on newly created accounts [ T1136 ], using built-in administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques. Once SafePay threat actors establish a foothold in a victim’s network, they use LOTL binaries (LOLBins) [ T1218 ], such as PsExec [ T1021.002 ] and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) [ T1021.006 ], to execute commands on remote systems. In several instances, SafePay threat actors used ShareFinder.ps1 —a PowerShell script function used for enumerating network file shares in Windows Active Directory environments—to identify valuable assets for exfiltration [ T1059.001 , T1059.003 ]. Additionally, SafePay threat actors used SharpShares.exe , a tool used to identify and enumerate network file shares. As SafePay threat actors prepare for lateral movement, they commonly disable security software [ T1685 ] to avoid detection. In some cases, the threat actors changed the passwords of system users, making valid logins impossible. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code [ T1027.002 ]. Privilege Escalation The authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors using a User Account Control (UAC) Bypass Privilege Escalation technique [ T1548.002 ] that creates an elevated process through a specified component object model, enabling the execution of malicious commands or binaries [ T1059 ]. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using token impersonation methods [ T1134.001 ]. Lateral Movement To pivot laterally through a network and identify files for exfiltration [ TA0010 ] and encryption, SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools like PsExec, WinRM, and Remote Management and Monitoring [ T1569.002 ] software. They also employ Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) [ T1021.001 , T1133 ] to expand their presence within the compromised network [ T1021 ]. As SafePay threat actors move laterally through a network, they look for credentials to gain admin access and will create accounts, if needed. Collection, Exfiltration, and Impact SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools, such as FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR to compress files and collect data [ T1560.001 ], and WinSCP and RClone to facilitate the exfiltration of data [ T1048 ] from the compromised network to actor-controlled accounts. In some instances, SafePay threat actors use OneDrive to exfiltrate data [ T1567 ]. In other instances, the SafePay threat actors installed legitimate remote desktop tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer on the victim’s systems. SafePay threat actors use these tools to transfer ransomware and other software onto a victim’s system. Additionally, SafePay threat actors halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset Network Attached Storage containing victim backup data to initial factory settings to inhibit system recovery attempts [ T1490 ]. Following exfiltration, SafePay threat actors encrypt files [ T1486 ] using a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange. This multilayered approach customizes encryption methods based on file type and size and enables full or partial encryption. Data encrypted with the SafePay ransomware variant (appended with .SafePay ) cannot be recovered without the decryption key. SafePay threat actors hold the encrypted data for ransom and typically demand a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software. SafePay threat actors leave a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal at a TOR .onion website link with a victim ID as the login. To put pressure on the victim, a representative makes phone calls on behalf of the ransomware group. If the victim does not pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to their SafePay leak website, which is linked in the ransom note. Following encryption, SafePay may delete itself from the victim’s filesystem [ T1070.004 ]. Leveraged Tools Table 1 lists publicly available tools and applications used by SafePay threat actors, including legitimate tools repurposed for their operations. Note: These tools and applications should not be attributed as malicious without analytical evidence to support threat actor use and/or control. Table 1. Tools Leveraged by SafePay Threat Actors Tool Name Description 7-Zip An open source software that enables users to compress various file formats. SafePay threat actors maliciously use 7-Zip for data packaging and movement. FileZilla An open source client that enables users to transfer files between servers. SafePay threat actors use FileZilla maliciously for data exfiltration. Mimikatz A credential dumper that enables users to view and save authentication credentials, such as Kerberos tickets [ T1550.002 ]. SafePay threat actors use Mimikatz for password exfiltration. PowerShell A cross-platform task automation solution used for various malicious activities, including command execution. It is composed of a command-line shell, a scripting language, and a configuration management framework—which runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. PsExec A tool designed to run programs that SafePay threat actors use to execute commands on remote systems. RClone A legitimate command-line program used to sync files with cloud storage services, such as Mega. SafePay threat actors maliciously use RClone for data packaging and movement. ScreenConnect A remote support, access, and meeting software that allows users to control devices remotely over the internet. SafePay threat actors use ScreenConnect for persistence and access. ShareFinder.ps1 A PowerShell script used to scan an Active Directory network for shared folders. SafePay threat actors use ShareFinder.ps1 for exfiltration hunting. WinRAR Archive utility used to split compromised data into segments and to compress [ T1560.001 ] files into a .RAR format prior to exfiltration. SafePay threat actors use WinRAR for data packaging and movement. WinRM A Windows-based protocol designed to facilitate remote management and automation. SafePay threat actors use WinRM for command execution. AnyDesk and TeamViewer Legitimate remote desktop tool used for accessing and controlling computers over the internet. SafePay threat actors use AnyDesk and TeamViewer to transfer malware to the victim’s system. AcronisDiskDirector A legitimate disk management tool. SharpShares.exe A network scanning tool used for host discovery and enumeration. NetExec A legitimate network assessment tool to enumerate systems, validate credentials, and manage remote operations across private networks. Backblaze A command-line tool for file management within Backblaze B2 cloud storage. SafePay threat actors executed commands via b2.exe to exfiltrate a victim’s data. Indicators of Compromise Table 2 through Table 5 list IOCs associated with SafePay ransomware that allowed for the identification of malicious activity. Incident Response If a potential compromise is detected, but ransomware actors have not (yet) encrypted items, organizations should take the following actions: Determine which hosts were compromised and isolate them by quarantining or taking them offline. Initiate threat hunting activities to scope the intrusion . Collect and review relevant artifacts, logs, and other data to identify threat actor TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, a timeline of activity, etc. Report the suspected compromise to the FBI and other agencies as appropriate (if located within the U.K., report the compromise to Report Fraud or local police force ) (see the Reporting section for contact information). Apply eviction countermeasures , including those listed below, to contain the incident and eradicate the threat actor from the network ( Note: Start applying countermeasures after collecting enough threat hunting data to inform effective countermeasure selection; this will likely overlap with threat hunting activities). Use CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool to assemble countermeasures for a systematic eviction plan—the tool comprises Playbook-NG (a web application) and COUN7ER (a database of post-compromise countermeasures mapped to adversary TTPs). Use Playbook-NG and COUN7ER together to assemble a systematic eviction plan, or playbook, that leverages distinct countermeasures to contain and evict cyber threat actors. The playbook features a list of recommended response actions based on threat actor TTPs and includes each action’s intended outcome, preparatory steps, and associated risks. For more information, see CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool fact sheet. Harden the network to prevent additional malicious activity (see Mitigations for guidance). If compromise is detected and items have been encrypted, see the “Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist” in CISA’s joint #StopRansomware Guide . Mitigations The authoring agencies recommend organizations implement the mitigations below to improve their cybersecurity posture on the basis of the threat actors’ activity. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures. Visit CISA’s CPGs webpage for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections. Organizations should implement the following mitigations: Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date , as timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats; specifically, prioritize patching KEVs in internet-facing systems. [ CPG 2.B ]. Additionally, using Binding Operational Directive 26-04 offers a framework for patch prioritization based on technology type and steps for forensics triage. Under its implementation guidance, it offers guidance and steps to perform forensic triage for severe vulnerability cases. Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all services to the greatest extent possible—particularly for webmail, VPNs, and accounts that access critical systems [ CPG 3.F ]. Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service accounts, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to comply with NIST’s digital identity guidelines ; require employees to use long passwords and consider not requiring recurring password changes, as these can weaken security [ CPG 3.B ]. Use longer passwords consisting of at least 15 characters and no more than 64 characters in length. Store passwords in a hashed format using industry-recognized password managers. Add password user “salts” to shared login credentials. Avoid reusing passwords [ CPG 3.C ]. Implement multiple failed login attempt account lockouts [ CPG 3.E ]. Disable password “hints.” Refrain from requiring password changes more frequently than once per year. Note: NIST guidance suggests favoring longer passwords instead of requiring frequent password resets. Frequent password resets are more likely to result in users developing password patterns cyber threat actors can easily decipher. Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes [ CPG 3.O ]; implementing this practice helps organizations avoid severe operational interruptions and prevents scenarios in which data is irretrievable. Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure [ CPG 3.K ]. Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (e.g., hard drives, storage devices, or the cloud) [ CPG 3.I , 3.O , 1.C ]. Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware, as network segmentation can help control traffic flows between, and access to, various subnetworks and restrict adversary lateral movement [ CPG 3.I ]. Identify, detect, and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool [ CPG 4.B ]. To aid in detecting ransomware, implement a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a network. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for detecting lateral connections as they have insight into common and uncommon network connections for each host. Filter network traffic by preventing unknown or untrusted origins from accessing remote services on internal systems—this prevents threat actors from directly connecting to remote access services that they have established for persistence. Review domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directories for new, unactive and/or unrecognized accounts. Disable unused ports . Consider adding an email banner to emails received from outside of your organization. Audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of least privilege [ CPG 3.G ]. Implement time-based access for accounts set at the admin level and higher ; for example, the Just-in-Time (JIT) access method provisions privileged access when needed and can support enforcement of the principle of least privilege (as well as the Zero Trust Maturity Model ). This is a process where a network-wide policy is set in place to automatically disable admin accounts at the Active Directory level when the account is not in direct need. Individual users may submit their requests through an automated process that grants them access to a specified system for a set timeframe when they need to support the completion of a certain task. Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions, since privilege escalation and lateral movement often depend on software utilities running from the command line; if threat actors cannot run these tools, they will have difficulty escalating privileges and moving laterally [ CPG 3.M ]. These mitigations align with principles provided in the joint guide Shifting the Balance of Cybersecurity Risk: Principles and Approaches for Secure by Design Software . CISA urges software manufacturers to take ownership of improving the security outcomes of their customers by applying these and other secure by design tactics. By implementing secure by design tactics, software manufacturers can make their product lines secure “out of the box” without requiring customers to make additional configuration changes, purchasing product security add-in software and logs, monitoring, and making frequent security updates. Validate Security Controls In addition to applying mitigations, the authoring agencies recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory. To get started: Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 6 to Table 16 ). Align your security technologies against the technique. Test your technologies against the technique. Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance. Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data. Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process. The authoring agencies recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory. Resources Stopransomware.gov is a whole-of-government approach that provides one central location for ransomware resources and alerts. CISA’s #StopRansomware Guide provides organizations with comprehensive best practices to mitigate the risk of ransomware attacks. CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog is an authoritative resource for organizations to support improvement of their patch management best practices. CISA’s Multifactor Authentication webpage provides best practices for network defenders to mitigate threats to accounts and systems that use MFA. CISA’s Cyber Hygiene Services help organizations reduce the risk of a successful cyberattack. USSS’s Preparing for a Cyber Incident outlines basic steps an organization can take before, during, and after a cyber incident. CISA’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) provides a systematic, disciplined, and repeatable approach for evaluating an organization’s security posture; see Downloading and Installing CSET for step-by-step guidance to help your organization evaluate cybersecurity practices on your networks. CISA’s Ransomware Risk Assessment helps assess an organization’s ability to counteract a ransomware infection. Department of Health and Human Services’ Cybersecurity Performance Goals is a resource to help healthcare organizations implement high-impact cybersecurity practices. CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and its implementation guidance CISA’s CI Fortify: Strengthening Resilience Across Critical Infrastructure CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool enables incident response teams to quickly turn observed behaviors into remediation plans U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre U.K.’s National Crime Agency Reporting Your organization has no obligation to respond or provide information to the FBI and other authoring agencies in response to this joint advisory. If, after reviewing the information provided, your organization decides to provide information to the FBI or other authoring agencies, reporting must be consistent with applicable state and federal laws. The FBI and other authoring agencies are interested in any information, to include boundary logs showing communication to and from foreign IP addresses, a sample ransom note, communications with threat actors, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files, and/or a benign sample of an encrypted file. Additional details of interest include a targeted company point of contact, status and scope of infection, estimated loss, operational impact, transaction IDs, date of infection, date detected, initial attack vector, and host- and network-based indicators. The authoring agencies do not encourage paying ransom as payment does not guarantee victim files will be recovered. Furthermore, payment may also embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or fund illicit activities. Regardless of whether you or your organization have decided to pay the ransom, the FBI and CISA urge you to promptly report ransomware incidents to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) , a local FBI field office , a local USSS Field Office , or CISA via the agency’s Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center ( contact@cisa.dhs.gov ) or by calling 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). In the U.K., report incidents of a cybercrime or fraud at the UK’s Home for Reporting Cyber Crime & Fraud or 0300-123-2040, your local police force , or use the non-emergency number 101. Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. CISA and the FBI/USSS do not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. Any reference to specific commercial entities, products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply endorsement, recommendation, or favoring by the FBI, CISA, or USSS. The authoring agencies recognize that infrastructure used for malicious activity may be hosted on cloud or virtualized platforms where IP addresses can be dynamically or temporarily assigned. As a result, an address associated with malicious activity at one point in time may later be reassigned to benign services. Accordingly, these indicators should be interpreted as historically observed infrastructure within the activity window and should be corroborated with current network telemetry or additional intelligence sources when used for defensive or investigative purposes. summary: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96652 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 Plex Media Server Improper Neutralization of Encoded URI Schemes in a Web Page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 Plex Media Server External Control of File Name or Path Vulnerability CVE-2026-106931 EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-110936 Siemens Software Center Uncontrolled Search Path Element Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: CVSSv3 Score: 9.8 CVE-2026-109618PHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).CVE-2026-109619PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE). summary: Update October 26, 2026: CISA has updated this Alert to reflect the addition of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Oct. 26, 2026. Update October 23, 2026 : CISA has updated this Alert to: (1) provide a SIGMA detection rule to help identify potentially suspicious activity; (2) incorporate partner resources; and (3) reinforce existing mitigation guidance. Purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 . These vulnerabilities, known as “php2shell,” allow for unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP. The vulnerabilities affect all PHP installations serving web requests, including Apache with mod_php ( Note : PHP considers this highest risk), PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. Organizations should immediately update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to fix these vulnerabilities. CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its KEV Catalog on Oct. 26, 2026. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify and inventory systems running any version of PHP across your organization. PHP is often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable. Apply the patch immediately, prioritizing internet-facing systems. Organizations that cannot update immediately, or that continue to use PHP 8.1 or earlier unsupported versions, should take PHP-based systems offline until they can be patched or updated. A web application firewall may provide some protection until systems are updated or patched. Review the official PHP security advisory for guidance on patching. Monitor for suspicious activity, including PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools. summary: Overview On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges. CVE CVSSv4 Description CVE-2026-109618 9.2 (Critical) RCE via OOM corruption CVE-2026-109619 9.2 (Critical) RCE via stale global state All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs. The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon. Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles. Multiple public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are now available. Rapid7 researchers have reviewed these and observe that each demonstrates RCE only against a specific combination of operating system, PHP version, and web server, and none appears to be broadly reliable. Rapid7’s own research supports this. Our attempts so far have produced a working exploit only under narrow lab conditions, and exploitation depends on assumptions that are unlikely to hold on internet-facing instances. We are continuing to investigate approaches that could improve portability, but have not yet developed a reliable, general-purpose exploit. Rapid7 has not observed exploitation in the wild, though there are multiple reports of exploitation attempts, which is expected for a vulnerability of this profile. The situation is evolving quickly, and a more portable exploit technique could emerge at any time. The current difficulty of reliable exploitation should be treated as a window to patch rather than a reason to delay, and Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis. Technical overview CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling According to the OOM advisory , PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM. Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. The advisory reports RCE over HTTP with default PHP input and memory limits, including multi-worker prefork deployments. PHP-FPM terminates a worker when startup fails, preventing that particular sequence. Source analysis supports FPM susceptibility after successful startup, but the advisory reports no complete FPM exploit for this CVE. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior, and memory layout. CVE-2026-109619: Use after free across requests PHP can reuse a worker process to handle multiple HTTP requests. The stale-state advisory describes internal state that still points to memory freed at the end of an earlier request. A later request handled by the same worker can access that stale value before normal initialization clears it. Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset. The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start() . The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition. Mitigation guidance PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions: PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35 PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36 PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27 PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12 Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4 , 8.0 , and 8.1 . Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement , or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source. Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation. PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment: For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit. For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini , an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern. Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length . If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP. Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA , which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path. For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting , display_errors , log_errors , or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe. For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and stale global state advisory . Rapid7 customers To learn how to use Rapid7 capabilities to find systems affected by these vulnerabilities and for answers to common questions, read the PHP2Shell documentation . For Rapid7 Customers with questions regarding Rapid7 products and their usage of PHP please consult this page. Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with remote unauthenticated vulnerability checks, available in a dedicated release that followed the regular October 21 content release. Rapid7 has also released authenticated scan checks for both the Scan Engine and the Agent for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as part of the October 22 content release. Authenticated, package-based checks are now available for a variety of Linux distributions. These checks evaluate installed distribution packages, so they can recognize backported fixes that keep the original upstream PHP version number. Run an authenticated scan with this content release to use them. For the full list of checks and supported distribution versions, read Rapid7’s PHP2Shell documentation , where package-based coverage for other distributions will be added as their fixes are published. In a dedicated October 23 content release following the regular release, Rapid7 has released coverage for CVE-2026-115560, published on October 23 by the PHP Foundation. A mitigation technique is available, but no patch has yet been published. Exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 relies on non-standard configuration. Current scope for authenticated coverage: macOS and Linux. Windows to follow. Remote unauthenticated coverage provides coverage regardless of web-server OS. Velociraptor A Velociraptor Artifact Generic.Applications.PHPInventory is available to inventory PHP installations on Windows, Linux and macOS for remediation scoping. This artifact allows for the collection of package versions, common binary and module paths, and running PHP processes. Updates October 21, 2026: Initial publication. summary:
A vulnerability in the interprocess communication (IPC) channel of the Secure Firewall Posture module in Cisco Secure Client could allow an authenticated, local attacker to elevate privileges on an affected device. This vulnerability is due to insufficient validation of user-supplied input. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a series of crafted IPC messages to a local socket. Although this vulnerability affects the Secure Firewall Posture module in Cisco Secure Client on Windows, macOS, and Linux operating systems, this vulnerability could be used to obtain full root privileges on macOS and Linux. summary:
A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root . This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies. Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated. An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device. Note: Cisco Expressway Series refers to Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) devices and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) devices. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. summary:
A vulnerability in the IPv4 packet processing functionality of Cisco IOS XR Software that affects Cisco ASR 9000 and 9900 Series Aggregation Services Routers as well as Cisco ASR 9902 and 9903 Compact High-Performance Routers could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause network processor (NP) errors, resulting in a line card reset or shutdown and a denial of service (DoS) condition. This vulnerability is due to the incorrect handling of crafted IPv4 packets that are received on an affected line card interface and processed as for-us traffic. The issue can result in an NP reset, causing traffic loss on the affected line card while it recovers. Under repeated reset conditions, the network processor may enter a persistent shutdown state, in which case an explicit line card reload may be required to restore traffic. The vulnerability is within the IPv4 packet-processing path. Transit IPv4 traffic does not trigger this issue and IPv6 traffic cannot trigger it. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-asr9k-tUyxcyXN

A vulnerability in the Snort 3 Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) Decompression Engine of multiple Cisco products could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the Snort 3 Detection Engine to restart unexpectedly, resulting in a denial of service (DoS) condition. This vulnerability is due to improper range checking when Snort 3 decompresses VBA data, which is user controlled. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted VBA data to the Snort 3 Detection Engine of a targeted device. summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-114625 Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator SQL Injection Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days. For security teams already managing growing vulnerability backlogs, this creates a difficult question: How do you reduce exposure when attackers can exploit vulnerabilities before your next patching window? Rapid7's Q3 2026 research brings together vulnerability intelligence, ransomware activity, APT tracking, and underground forum intelligence to show where attacker activity is concentrated. The exploitation window has narrowed, big time Rapid7 tracked 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities this quarter, down 7% from Q2 but still 19% higher than the same period last year. The number of newly exploited vulnerabilities isn't growing at the same rate as disclosures. The more pressing concern is how quickly attackers exploit the vulnerabilities they choose. On average, exploitation occurred just three days after public disclosure. The report also found that 80% of tracked exploitation occurred within 14 days and 90% within 30 days. That timeline creates a serious challenge for organizations relying on fixed remediation schedules. It also reinforces the need to distinguish between vulnerabilities that are theoretically severe and those that pose an immediate, exploitable risk. The report examines the exploitation timeline in greater detail, including the vulnerability characteristics that make certain exposures particularly attractive to attackers. Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities tracked, 34 (79%) required no authentication or user interaction. This provides attackers a potential path into exposed systems, no stolen credentials or malicious content interaction necessary. An internet-facing service with an exploitable vulnerability may require immediate attention, particularly when an attacker can reach it without authenticating. This makes attack surface visibility and contextual prioritization essential. Security teams need to understand which systems are externally accessible, which vulnerabilities are actively exploited, and whether existing controls can prevent or limit compromise. A CVSS score alone won’t give you the answers. The report explores the characteristics of exploited vulnerabilities and why understanding reachability is critical to reducing risk. AI is taking on a more operational role in attacks In Q3, 8% of the threat reporting tracked by Rapid7 cited AI as an operational component. The research identifies a shift from using AI primarily to help draft content or code toward supporting tactical decisions and execution within attack campaigns. In the documented cases, human operators continued to select targets and determine objectives, but relied on AI assistance for technique selection, target assessment, and adapting when an attack step failed. The report also examines how threat actors split malicious objectives across multiple AI sessions to evade provider safeguards. There are serious implications for detection in these findings. AI-enabled attacks also reinforce the value of monitoring and quickly adapting to attacker behavior rather than relying exclusively on known malware signatures or threat actor identities. The report provides additional context on how AI appeared in tracked campaigns and what defenders should monitor. The next step: Prioritize exposure before attackers exploit it Q3's findings reveal a challenge that vulnerability counts alone can’t explain. Attackers exploited 43 newly tracked vulnerabilities this quarter, yet the average exploitation window was just three days. Meanwhile, underground forum monitoring identified 41 posts advertising RDP or network access, demonstrating continued interest in selling access to compromised environments. Security teams must account for both the vulnerabilities attackers can exploit directly and the access they can obtain through other means. Start by identifying externally accessible assets and the vulnerabilities affecting them. Prioritize known exploitation, unauthenticated access paths, and systems supporting critical business functions. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, assess compensating controls and detection coverage. The latest Rapid7 Quarterly Threat Landscape Report brings together vulnerability research, ransomware intelligence, nation-state activity, and dark web monitoring to help security teams understand where threats are concentrated and what to address first. Download and read it now .

summary: On 20 October 2026, the PHP project announced an upcoming security release addressing two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. Public reports indicated that these vulnerabilities could lead to remote code execution (RCE). The PHP team released the fixes today, 21 October 2026 at 13:30 UTC, in PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Both vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Technical details are now being discussed publicly, and initial proofs of concept (PoCs) have begun to circulate. This raises the likelihood that attackers are already exploiting the vulnerabilities. [New] On 23 October, PHP disclosed a new RCE vulnerability. However, it affects only web applications configured in an unusual way, and PHP considers it an unlikely risk. PHP will not issue an out-of-band release for this vulnerability. Instead, organisations are advised to apply mitigation to fully protect from this RCE vector. CERT-EU advises organisations to patch affected assets immediately. Where that is not feasible, organisations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is applied and verified.

summary:
Between October 17 and October 20, 2026, a critical security compromise involving Certificate Authorities that are managed by eMudhra was uncovered. A security researcher demonstrated that the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were fundamentally broken due to an unprecedented error in their Key Generation Ceremony (KGC) in April 2025. This allows anyone to brute-force acquire these private keys within seconds. For more information, see eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise and the Cisco Talos blog post Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates . Important: If a product is not listed within this advisory, Cisco's review indicates that the product is not affected by this vulnerability. This advisory will be updated as additional information becomes available. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-emudhra-info-ScS22A1r
Security Impact Rating: Informational

summary: Multiple vulnerabilities have been discovered in PHP, the most severe of which could allow for remote code execution. PHP is a widely-used, open-source server-side scripting language designed primarily for web development. All PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed are considered at risk. Successful exploitation of the most severe of these vulnerabilities could allow for unauthenticated remote code execution in the context of the affected service account. Depending on the privileges associated with the service account, an attacker could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full user rights. Services whose accounts are configured to have less rights on the system could be less impacted than those who operate with administrative user rights.

General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. [1] SSVC SSVCv2/E:N/A:N/2026-09-28T14:29:30Z/ Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the exploitation risk of this vulnerability. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, and ensure they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolate them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as its connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. summary: View CSAF Summary Nozomi Networks has published information on vulnerabilities in Nozomi Guardian/CMC. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by these vulnerabilities. Siemens recommends to contact customer support to receive patch and update information. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices are affected: RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389, CVE-2026-33391, CVE-2026-33920) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 4 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine, Incorrect Authorization, Lack of Administrator Control over Security, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-33387 A template injection vulnerability was discovered in the Dashboards functionality due to improper validation of an input parameter. An authenticated user with the required privileges can define a dashboard containing a malicious payload, or a victim can be socially engineered into importing a malicious dashboard. When the victim views or imports the dashboard, the payload executes in their browser context, allowing the attacker to modify application data or disrupt application availability. Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-1336 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 4.6 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33388 An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Credentials Manager functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. A remote authenticated user with limited privileges can view a limited subset of the available entries in the Credentials Manager. The actual credential values are not directly visible, but the user can delete entries or edit their properties. An attacker who deletes or edits an entry can disrupt authentication for dependent devices, and one who manipulates an entry's configuration may be able to indirectly obtain the credentials. Read More 2 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.4 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33389 An improper certificate/host key validation vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling functionality, which established encrypted connections to target devices without validating the remote host's identity, and no option was provided to enable it. A man-in-the-middle attacker positioned between a sensor and a polled device can, during a polling session, impersonate the device and intercept the communication, including the credentials used to access it. The captured credentials can then be replayed to authenticate against the device itself or against other devices sharing the same credentials, allowing the attacker to access and tamper with the device's data and to disrupt its operations. summary: View CSAF Summary Siemens Industrial Edge Devices contain multiple path traversal vulnerabilities that could facilitate an authenticated remote attacker to access sensitive internal information. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. vulnerabilities to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. General Recommendations As a general security measure Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to affected products with appropriate mechanisms. It is advised to follow recommended security practices in order to run the devices in a protected IT environment. Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, and ensure they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolate them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. summary: View CSAF Summary RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) contains multiple vulnerabilities in the integrated SQLite component that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code, cause a denial of service, or obtain sensitive information. Siemens has released a new version for RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) and recommends to update to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller are affected: RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) vers:intdot/<6.0 (CVE-2025-6965, CVE-2025-70873, CVE-2025-71316, CVE-2026-11822, CVE-2026-11824) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) 4 Vulnerabilities Numeric Truncation Error, Improper Clearing of Heap Memory Before Release ('Heap Inspection'), Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding, Heap-based Buffer Overflow Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2025-6965 There exists a vulnerability in SQLite versions before 3.50.2 where the number of aggregate terms could exceed the number of columns available. This could lead to a memory corruption issue. We recommend upgrading to version 3.50.2 or above. Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Update to V6.0 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-197 Numeric Truncation Error CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.7 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2025-70873 An information disclosure issue in the zipfileInflate function in the zipfile extension in SQLite v3.51.1 and earlier allows attackers to obtain heap memory via supplying a crafted ZIP file. Read More 2 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Update to V6.0 or later version RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Update to V6.0 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-244 Improper Clearing of Heap Memory Before Release ('Heap Inspection') CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.5 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N View CVE Details CVE-2025-71316 SQLite 'sqldiff.exe' does not securely handle the way the Microsoft Windows C runtime converts Unicode characters to ANSI codepages. An attacker could use the '-L' option to load an arbitrary DLL with a crafted command line argument string that results in command line file arguments being misinterpreted as command line options. Fixed on or around 2025-12-26. Read More 3 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Update to V6.0 or later version RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Update to V6.0 or later version RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) < V6.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Update to V6.0 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-176 Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 9.8 CRITICAL CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details CVE-2026-11822 SQLite before 3.53.2 contains memory corruption vulnerabilities in the FTS5 full-text search extension that allow attackers to cause process crashes, memory exhaustion, or arbitrary code execution by supplying a crafted database with malformed FTS5 page data. Attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds read in fts5LeafSeek() via an attacker-controlled loop bound and a heap buffer overflow write in fts5ChunkIterate() through a crafted continuation page causing an integer underflow, exploitable when an FTS5 MATCH query is executed against the malicious database. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.
